entries.title: An Open Letter to Chancellor Young
entries.author: Ad Hoc Committee in Support of the Women's Resource Center and ten other campus groups
entries.text:
An Open Letter to Chancellor Young
Charies E. Young
May 23, 1978
Chancellor
University of California, Los Angeles
Dear Chancellor Young,
Representatives of each of the undersigned groups and other interested students attended the Registration
Fee Advisory Committee (Reg Fee) meeting on Wednesday, May 17, 1978. The representatives were there
to show support for the full continued funding of the UCLA Child Care Center and the Women's Resource
Center and to protest the Reg. Fee Committee's closed door procedures. In addition, hundreds of students
attended the April 6, 1978 Reg Fee meeting and the April 21, 1978 Board of Control meeting to support full
funding of the Child Care Center 1978-79 budget request which was granted.
We understand that the Reg. Fee Committee is plagued by budgetary concerns and that continual review of
programs funded by Reg. Fees is essential for maintaining programs which truely represent what students
want and need. We are very much concerned however that the needs of many students are not being
represented. These unrepresented students, while not a majority, are a significant and important group on
campus and include women, parents and minorities. This group has a demonstrated need for child care
and for the unique services provided by the Women's Resource Center. The recent action taken by the Reg.
Fee Committee represents a philosophy toward women and minorities which is in sharp contrast to the
goals of the University's Affirmative Action Plan.
Specifically, we wish to bring your attention to the following questions:
1) DISCRIMINATION: Is the Reg. Fee Committee responsible for only representing the white, childless,
male student? We believe the Reg. Fee recommendations do not represent the needs of women and nontraditional students.
2) IRRESPONSIBILITY AND CLOSED DOOR TACTICS: What justification is there for a body charged
with recommending the allocation of student funds to meet behind closed doors and to consider the
reduction or elimination of programs without notifying the departments under question? When interested
students and child care administrators were present to answer questions, the Child Care budget request
(which already included a 9.7% reduction) was approved with a modest.3% further reduction, bringing the
total approved request to a 10% decrease from the year before. (The total request is less than .004 of the
Total Reg. Fee budget). The matter was then reopened without notification to the Child Care Center and a
50% reduction in funding was approved. Similarly, despite the specific request of the Women's Resource
Center Director to be notified when the Reg. Fee Committee would be considering that budget, no
notification was made.
3) WOMEN'S RESOURCE CENTER. If the Women's Resource Center is eliminated where will students
learn about the changing role of women in today's society? The Women's Resource Center, in addition to
providing a comprehensive information and referral service is the only place on campus where women
students are able to identify and address their special needs.
4) FINANCIAL AIDS: Why does the Reg Fee Committee believe that the currently inadequate funds
available through Financial Aids will be sufficient to meet students child care costs? If the Child Care
Center is eliminated in favor of Family Day Care Homes, or if the recommendation that low income student
parents be charged fees is acted upon, over $67,000 in State Grant monies ( financial aids) will be forfeited
and that burden will be placed on the University's Financial Aid resources.
5) FAMILY DAY CARE PROGRAM: Why does the Reg. Fee Committee assume that Family Day Care
Homes can accomodate the 73 children in the Child Care Center and the 400 people on the waiting list?
This Program is a necessary and valuable component of the University's Child Care Services and is
meeting the needs of many UCLA families. However, it too has a growing waiting list, especially for infants
and toddlers where alternatives are virtually unavailable.
6) NEED: The 400 people on the Child Care Center waiting list clearly reflects the great need for this
service by many students. The Women's Resource Center addresses the needs of all students on campus
by increasing the awareness of the changing role of women and men in today's society, the women's
movement, the special needs of women, and the need to improve the status of women.
We urge you to address these pertinent questions and to reject the recommendations of the Reg. Fee
Committee. We further urge your support to the Child Care Services Administrative Staff in their efforts to
expand the available on-Campus Child Care. The U.C. Campuses at Irvine and Riverside have on-Campus
Centers specifically designed and constructed for child care. The campuses at Santa Cruz and San
Francisco are in the process of constructing new child care facilities. Next door to the existing UCLA
Center is the pest control storage building and parking lot. This space should be designated for a larger
child care facility with all of the University's efforts directed toward mobilizing available resources to make
adequate campus child care a reality.
Finally, we urge that the Child Care Center be given a three year funding commitment. The continual
reevaluation of the existence of the Child Care Center and the Women's Resource Center by non-elected
students is both inefficient and costly to all concerned.
Signed
Ad Hoc Committee in Support of the Women's Resource Center
Asian Coalition
Campuses United Against Apartheid
Child Care Center Parents and Staff
Committee in Support of Non-Traditional Students
Community Service
Graduate Women's History Association
National Organization for Women Campus Task Force
Student Coalition Against Racism
Together
Women in Law Society

entries.title: Child Care Center parents may sue UC
entries.author: Leone Cherksey
entries.text:
Child Care Center parents may sue UC
By Leone Cherksey
DB Staff Writer
ASUCLA Child Care Center parents
are contemplating a lawsuit against
the University in response to Chancellor Young's decisions regarding
Child Care Center governance, according to Teresa Birchard, head of
the Child Care Center Board
Governance.
Birchard said the suit would be
based on deprivation of federal or
state funds beeause of the University's
alleged failure to follow federal interagency day care standards. She said
thesè standards require a minimum of
50 per cent parent representation on
Child Care Advisory boards.
Young's committee composition
allows for one parent from each of the
f two child care centers. Since there is
presently one existing child care
center, this amounts to, one parent
member on an eight member committee.
Child Care Center parents are
willing to designate staff in addition to
parents as representatives, but they
want the two groups to add up to half
the committee, Birchard said.
Young's definition
In addition to the committee
composition issue, pareits disagree
with Young's definition of the Child
Care Committee's function. Young
stated in a letter to the University
Policies Commission, "The Child Care
Policy Advisory Committee is a policy
advisory committee to the Vice
Chancellor-Administration or his
designee." Child Care parents replied
with the motion, "Parents shall
continue to support the concept of a
policy decision-making board rather
than an advisory board." The motion
passed 23-1 in a parent meeting last ~
week. The committee also passed a
unanimous resolution calling for staff
representation on the committee.
Carry weight
James W. Hobson, Vice Chancellor-
Administration, who now has charge
of the Child Care Center, said the
University's structure does not permit
it to "give away" the responsibility of
governance. He added that advisory
committees have more weight than is
usually understood, and said likely
conflict between committee advice
and administrators is "quite limited."
Hobson said the Center will be
operated according to guidelines of the
State of California Department of
Education, which allocates federal
grants. He did not interpret these
guidelines to necessitate a change in
the Advisory Committee composition.
According to Birchard, parents want
a policy committee with high parental
representation to ensure children are
left "happily and safely" at the
Center. "We've been trying to get
some input for months," she said. "No
one has really thought about the
parents or the children."
Birchard said parents will
"definitely refuse to associate with the
policy committee" unless it is granted
more policy making power and
parent-staff representation. She
claimed parent rejection of 'Young's
deeisions was almost unanimous.
She alleged that Donald Findley,

Executive Director of ASUCLA, had
expressed to her prior to Young's
official statement that "he expected
there would be a few parents who
woald cause trouble but if they tried to
interfere in any way with the implementation that he assumed that
Hal Thompson (Executive Manager,
of Facilities and Operations) would have
their children expelled from the
Center." Findley denied making such
a statement.
UPC report
Birchard expressed preference for
the UPC report over Luke Fishburn's,
which was basically accepted by
Chancellor Young. She called Fishburn " a managerial consultant who
made non-managerial recommendations." She said his original draft
included passages "offensive to
parents"' such as advice to women of
che "potential human costs of child
Fishburn said the phrase about
potential human costs was removed DB Photos by Paul
from the report, not because he
believed there were none ("there are
human costs to everything," he added), but because parents objected.
Child Care Center parents sent to
politicians copies of letter to
Chancellór Young detailing their
objections to his decisions. Some included Mayor Thomas Bradley and
Senators John Tunney and Alan
Cranston. Birchard said the parents
hope to obtain help from these
representatives.

entries.title: Young plans campus child care phase-out
entries.author: Eric Mandel
entries.text:
Young plans campus child care phase-out

By Eric Mandel
DB Staff Writer
The demise of campus child care will come December 31,
if Chancellor Charles E. Young adheres to the consensus
reached during a meeting of administrators this week.
Young told the Bruin, "As of the moment we are trying
to work out an arrangement to phase out campus child
care by December 31." An off-campus home care program
will replace the on-campus facility if the administrative plan
is implemented.
• The decision to end on-campus child care services was
made during a Tuesday meeting between Young and other
campus administrators, including interim Child Care
Director Luke Fishburn and assistant Vice-Chancellor Hal
Thompson.
The meeting was prompted by the Registration Fee
Committeeis recommendation last week that offering child
care services through-an on-campus facility is too expensive
should be terminated. The Registration Fee
and
Committee, which advises the Chancellor on how to spend
the approximately $10 million collected.in student
registration fees each year, was the first of several funding
hurdles which child care administrators had to overcome.
Until Young met with his administrators, all of the
previous child care proposals had been made by the Child
Care Advisory Committee set up at the, beginning of this
year.
The most recent plan presented by the Advisory
Committee, the third to be rejected by Reg Fee, called for a
combination of both on- and off-campús child care
services.
When confronted with the high costs of an on-campus
facility, the Chancellor last week told Reg Fee and child
care administrators, "It's higher than educating students at
UCLA."
Interim Child Care Director Luke Fishburn argued to
Reg Fee that the on-campus center is still necessary,
because of the experimental nature of the outreach
program. In response, acting Reg Fee member Bill Cormier
expressed concern that the outreach experiment would fai]
and the University would be stuck with just the on-campus
facility.
After the decision to attempt to phase out the on-campus
center Fishburn expressed confidence in the outreach
program's ability to function with only administrative
offices and a referral service on campus. He said, "The
outreach program appears to have great potential for
. However, it is very

unfortunate."

entries.title: Child Care Supported
entries.text:
Child Care
Supported
(Editor's note: the following
letter was sent to Chancellor
Charles Young. Aug. 4)
We are writing in reply to your
decision to terminate UCLA's
Family Day Care Program and the
Child Care Center. We would like
to bring several points about the
Family Day Care Program to your
attention.
Since the inception of this
program 2½ years ago, 236 children of UCLA staff, faculty, and
students have received excellent
care in our homes. Presently, we
are caring for over 100 UCLA
children. While it is true that if
the Family Day Care Program
closes these children will continue to receive care, those parents
(approximately 25 per month)
who contact the Family Day Care
office staff and are seeking child
care will lose a valuable source of
UCLA child care referral and
placement.
September, December, and
June are months during which
the greatest numbers of parents
either terminate their children's
care or are actively seeking care
in our program. For example, in
1977, between June 30 and September 30, 180 parents called
requesting information on Family
Day Care, 30 children terminated
from our program and 53 children were placed in our homes
by thê Family Day Care staff. The
number of children in this program has doubled since•September of 1977, but without the
presence of the office staff to
arrange interviews with parents
and match children with providers, crucial fall placements as
well as subsequent placements

for UCLA parents will not take
place.
The demand for child care by
campus parents as indicated by
the waiting lists in both the Child
Care Center and the Family Day
Care Program reflects the demand for care that exists throughout the Los Angeles area. As
Family Day Care Providers, we
receive calls from many non-
UCLA parents who are urgently
requesting care in our homes. We
have explained to these parents
that we have contracted with
UCLA to accept UCLA children
that the program staff place in
qur homes. If this program ends
we will no longer give first priority to UCLA parents as openings
arise.
In a short period of time the
UCLA Family Day Care Program
has become nationally known.
We have opened our homes to
visitors from government and
educational institutions. One
researcher from HEW commented that our style of home care
,was. such an excellent form of
child care it should serve as the
model for other programs of this
kind across the country.
By our dedicated service to this
University, we have proven that
Family Day Care provides a stable, consistent, developmentally
beneficial type of care that is as
acceptable to parents as center
care.
Our growth and development
as providers is due to the support
and leadership of the staff of this
program. The service this staff
provides such as monthly visits to
•our homes to discuss concerns
we have about parents and. children, opportunities fer us to hear
guest speakers talk on child development, provisions for university
and community resources being
accessible to us are as essential as
the actual child care itself.
An office staff organize and
coordinate our efforts as providers and make known to parents
the vast range of services we
offer. These services include
choice of child care location
because our homes extend from
the San Fernando Valley south to
Redondo Beach and from Santa
Monica east to Hollywood. We
offer full and part.time care, night
and weekend care, and care for
children with special needs such
as handicapped.
Presently, there are 53 providers in this program. We have
potential spaces in our homes for
the care of over 100 ihfants. In
'fact half of the children in this
program are infants. We also
provide care for preschool children and afterschool care, and
pick up and delivery of children.
(Continued on Page 10)

the clout to hit back. I believe it
runs counter to every current
proposal that encourages
women, minorities, welfare
recipients, et al to obtain a higher
education and professional
degrees. Nor do l feel that Child
Care is a "frill" to be cut.
I.do hope that, with the actual
budget announced, the Chancellor will be able to review his
action and reinstate his allocation.— in accordance with the •
wishes of the students, as expressed in their campus election.
Anna Sherman Vineberg

entries.title: Child Care Committee praised
entries.author: Peter Lowber
entries.text:
Child Care Committee praised

After a year of fruitless attempts
Editor:
to establish a child care center
through the "channels", a group of
energetic parents, students, and
employees have organized a
voluntary day care center on their
own initiative. The center opened
on Monday in the Women's
Lounge.
About 30 kids of ages varying
from six months to pre-school age
played together. What had been
felt before as a need had been met
in fact for those people involved.
By the end of the day, parents who
had not been previously working
with the group were signing up
their kids for the rest of the week.
Meanwhile, the bureaucratic
wheels have been set in motion.
The bureaucracy only moves
when challenged. The need for a
child care center is not any greater
now than a year ago. The Child
Care Committee last year found
that students and employees at
UCLA had 2800 children under six
years of age. But this committee
never got beyond the proposal
stage, and of course the Administration, led by Chancellor
Young, ignored every proposal.
However, the Administration could
not ignore direct action. When
the
confronted directly,
bureaucracy is forced to react.
And so it has reacted.
The arm of the bureaucracy in
this case is ASUCLA. In response
to the voluntary child care center,
Don Findley, executive director of
ASUCLA, has drawn up a proposal
offering University facilities for a
child care center available by next
April. The Administration would
agree to donate temporary use of
the horticulture building for a
three-year experimental period.
However, the agreement is not
being made between the Administration and the present Child

Care Center; rather it is being hc
made between the Administration
8
and the Administration (i.e. bet- m
ween Chancellor Young and
ASUCLA ).
Chancellor Young has had the
arrogance to say that "I am
pleased that ASUCLA has
volunteered to bring the project to
fruition since it is the logical
agency to respond to this need of
the campus community." The
LOGICAL agency! Indeed!!! For
Chancellor Young what could be
more logical! But what about the
present Child Care Center?? What
could be a more logical "agency"
than those people who are most
directly involved in fighting to
satisfy their needs?
Not only is the Administration
trying to ignore the child care
center now operating, but it is
demanding that this center get out
of the Woman's Lounge after
Friday without offering it any
alternative site. Meanwhile, the
child care center it is offering
through Findley will not be open
until April. Furthermore, it will be
limited to 60-80 children. The
Administration has not said whose
children will be allowed access to
this center, nor have they said how
it will be staffed.
These details will be worked out
by a committee of at least five
members, only three of whom will
be from the present Child Care
Center. Furthermore, the Administration will have veto power
over whatever this , committee
decides anyway.
Despite the machinations of the
bureaucracy, the Child Care
Committee has already won a
victory. This week's experience
has brought people together in a
common struggle. The daily
barriers of alienation have been
broken, and the group has won a
concession from the Administration. At the same time,

lowever, I would hope that the
group does not allow the Adninistration to swallow them.
Peter Lowber
Grad, History

entries.title: Keep child center
entries.author: Rima Jodele
entries.text:
Keep child center
Editor:
Help! I will be forced to drop
out of school if the UCLA Child
Care Center is no longer funded
after this June. The UCLA Child
Care Center meets the needs of
students in a manner that ordinary child care centers and nursery schools do not. There are
many of us
who are trying to

one of the most appreciated
student services on campus."

entries.title: [Letter in support of the Child Care Center]
entries.author: Lesley Ann Kawaguchi
entries.text:
Editor:
Are the students of UCLA
aware of the possible demise. of
the ASUCLA Child Care Center?*
The male dominated Reg Fee
Committee seems to feel that
women's place is still in the
home. Instead of voting to extend
Child Care services at UCLA, to
begin to include the children of
all UCLA student-parents, the
committee is considering withdrawing support from the Child
Care Center.
Once again, an insensitive
funding committee, in search of
ways to save money, focuses its
attention on withdrawing funds
from an agency designed, in part,
to answer the needs of women
students and their children.
Rather thanrecognize the essential service to UCLA women
the Child Care Center provides,
one member of the committee
was heard to remark that "support. of the UCLA Child Care
Center encourages irresponsibility and promiscuity." Does this
imply that this committee member fears irresponsible and
promiscuous conduct in the one
to four year old range?
Students, help control the
allocation of your monies. Attend
the Reg Fee Committee Meeting,
tonight at 5 p.m., Regents Dining
Hall, 2nd Floor Murphy. Support
the Child Care Center.
Lesley Ann Kawaguchi
Graduate, History

entries.title: Reg Fees vetoes funding; end to child care here?
entries.author: Eric Mandel and Patrick Healy
entries.text:
Reg Fees vetoes
end to child care
By Eric Mandel and Patrick Healy
DB Staff Writers
The doom-of campus child care may
have been sealed this week when the
Registration Fee Committee voted to reject
the Child Care Center proposal prepared
by administrators and an advisory committee.
This plan, the third to be thrown out by
Reg Fee this year, was termed "a go or nogo proposition" by Vice Chancellor James
Hobson, whose office currently oversees
campus child care services.
• Reg Fee objected mainly to the high cost
of child care. In a Tuesday meeting with
the Child Care Advisory Committee and
University administrators, including Chancellor Charles E. Young, the Registration
Fee Committee voted four to three against
implementing an expanded child care
program next January. At the same time,
Reg Fee voted $23,332 in funds to last the
Child Care Center through the end of this
year. Although Reg Fee said it still will
considér- revised child care proposals,
observers predicted that the Committee's
vote effectively will lead to a phasing out
of the current Child Care Center. Former Reg
Fee member and current student body president
Lindsay Conner said that in all probability Reg
Fee had made a "cut-off vote," because it has no
guarantee that the funds will be available later if
it changes its mind.
-No power
Reg Fee does not have the power to alloçate
funds, but merely makes recommendations to
Chancellor Young about how the approximately
$10 million in student fees should be spent each
year. However, in most cases Young follows the
Committee's advice.
The majority of Reg Fee members at the
meeting strongly objected to the high cost per
child of the on-campus child care facility, which
in all three plans amöunted to between $3,500
and $4,000 per child per year. Robert Rivero,
an acting Reg Fee member, was alarmed to find

so little progress had been made in the five
years UCLA has been trying to develop an
efficient child care service. "You've gone
through all this (to lower the cost) and it's still
$4,000 per child (per year)," he said.
After the meeting, Assistant Vice Chancellor proposal will have an annual cost of $460 per
Cello T. Hopefuly, itl ivl wak to the chere.
asking for." Thompson is the man in Hobson's
office who is diiectly esponsible for child care.
. However, Young did not appear sympathetic
to child care at Tuesday's meetings. After
listening to the complaints of Registration Fee
members that the child care proposals presented
so far are too expensive (with a total year cost of
around half a million dollars), Young rose from
his chair and responded, "I agree with you.
That's why I had to be brought kicking and

screaming into child care. I knew this is where
we'd be five years later." The chancellor then left
the meeting.
The latest Child Care Advisory Committee
child for the 1975-76 fiscal year. It would be
about $295 for the next year. Money is saved
through the use of an outreach program in which
children are cared for in private homes.
Included in the plan is a provision for
continuing the on-campus facility, which is what
many. Reg. Fee members object to. Interim Child
Care Center Director Luke Fishburn said the oncampus center is necessary to the outreach
program. "The off-campus care is kind of an
experimental thing and I would hate to close it
down until we are sure the outreach program is
working," he said.

entries.title: Noble administrators will raze Child Care
entries.text:
Noble administrators
will raze Child Care
Editor:
The dust has not yet cleared
from the uproar caused by the
passage of Proposition 13, and yet
our administrators at UCLA have
almost fallen over each other in
their eagerness to terminate the
Child Care Center. Rather than
admit that they have never
- approved of or supported the
Center, they claim that Proposition 13 requires a re-assessment
of all University services and thus
the excuse to close the child care'
facility.
No one has informed the
University about the precise
impact of Proposition 13 or the
relationship between Proposition
13 and the monies of the Reg Fee
Committee or ASUCLA. Even
more revealing, no other University facility has been closed by
the administration using Proposition 13 as the scape-goat.
As a consolation prize, the
noble adminstrators note that
they will not raze the Child Care
Center buildings and will allow
student-parents the option of a
co-operative school. Let me
propose an alternative solution

that will not onty serve the
financial needs of this university
but will give students on this
campus valuable learning experience. Why not make the
university administration a cooperative venture? We would
save hundreds of thousands of
dollars in salaries with the added
benefit of allowing students;
interested in learning about
adrninstrative work, on the job
training. With all of the money
saved, we could fund a child.care
center quadruple the size of the
existing facility.
Far fetched you say? No more
far-fetched than asking full time
UCLA student-parents to take on
the added responsibility of
running a school for their children. A university funded child
care center is not some luxury to
be trifled with when financial
whims strike. A quality child care
center is a necessary service—it
insures that a diverse population
can attend this university while
providing quality care for our
children.
Sharon V. Salinger
Grad-history

entries.title: Reconsider Child Care
entries.author: Kathleen Fellers
entries.text:
Reconsider
Child Care
Editor: An open letter to Chancellor-Young:
I am appalled to learn that you
have decided to withdraw all'
support for the Child Care
Center: that you have chosen to
support the leisure time activities
of a pampered majority and to
ignore, with the blithe disregard
of the well-situated, the very real
needs of hardworking, temporarily disadvantaged (but feepaying) student parents:
This is a model center with an
excellent reputation in a forward
looking field that has become
increasingly important in today's
world. Care of this fine calibre
cannot be found in the commercial marketplace and the experience of this facility provides
valuable data to a burgeoning
area of nationwide concern -
quality child care for parents who
cannot afford to stay at home.
Where is UCLA's pride in that?
The Center provides an invaluable educational arena that is
unduplicated in the commercial
world for early childhood development studies - accessible to
the medical school and the
departments of speech, psychology, and lingustics, to name only
a few. Where is UCLA's vision as a
coordinator of university resources?
My taxes have helped support
this university for many years and
have paid for myriad activities
which not only have been of no
benefit to me but also have been
of substantially less-than-compel-

ling social importance. The
existence of the Child Care
- Center was an important factor in
-my choice to come to UCLA.
When graduate from the law
school in 1980, I won't need this
service any longer but there will
be many others like me who will.
I urge you to reconsider your
position on this issue for the sake
of the many individuals and
interests who will lose by your
, recent decision.
Kathleen-Fellers

entries.title: Fishy
entries.text:
Fishy
Editor:
If I did not know that, many
people would take seriously
Luke Fishburn's article (Oct. 8
DB) on the proposed home day
care system, I would find it
merely amusing.
First of all, Luke is referred to
as the former Child Care Center
director even though he served
,in that capacity despite his lack
of the qualifications mandated
by the California Administrative
Code and justified this by using
the Center's administrative assistant, who was provisionally
certified, as. a sham.
• Since the time Luke was originally hired as a child care
consultant in June 1974, he has
been very hostile to group child
care. He has said that women
should choose between having
children and working. or going
to school. If they have children,
they should stay at home and be
• full-time mothers. He asked women questions like, "How can
you justify to your husband
leaving your child in a child care
center?"
Luke first referred to the caretakers as "trained" then in a
later paragraph as "unskilled."
"Unskilled" may be more accurate, but even this points to
his personal aversion to the.
concept of affirmative action for
wo,men:
If these women are unskilled
they should be given the opportunity to develop skills. It is
immoral to build a national day
care program on the assumption
that there will be a larger force
of unskilled married women.
Home day care is not a new
idea for this area. On the con-

nature of most existing day care
homes and see no concrete proposals to improve upon this in
UCLA's proposed program:
Just remember that the focal
point is the difference in cost
between satisfactory on-campus
day care which is beneficial to
children, and off-campus care of
doubtful values.
Who loses? The children, of
course, and the next generation
will pay for today's economizing.
Teresa Thomas Birchard
Law student

Child care meets with funding problems
By Patrick Mandealy
DB Staff Reporter
With • the 1975-76 fiscal year less than three
months away, and amidst indications that two of
three funding sources for child care services at this
campus may not come up with the full financial
backing expected of them, the Child Care Advisory
Committee is still trying to develop an acceptable - what Reg Fee may decide," BOC Chairman Ron
proposal for the Child Care Center in the coming
year.
The current outline, for child care, which is now
administered by the University rather than the
Associated Students (ASUCLA), calls for funding
from ASUCLA, student registration fees and
Chancellor's funds. These monies are necessary to
pay the expected $200,000 deficit not covered bý
parents' fees and a state grant.
The Registration Fee Committee (Reg Fee),
however, has balked at coming up with the
requested $62,972. Reg Fee had several objections to
the original child care proposal for next year and
last month asked the advisory committee to submit
a revised child care plan with a higher benefit/cost
ratio. The original proposal projected serving approximately 150 children at a total yearly cost of
around half a million dollars.

While the advisory committee is working on its
new proposal, with the completion date targeted for
the first of May, the Board of Control (BOC), which
will make the final decision on the $62,972 requested
from ASUCLA, has indicated it may not accept the
new child care plan.
"We will make our own decision, independently of
Sufrin said. He added that BOC may decide to
allocate only a portion of the requested total.
On the possibility that the advisory committee
may not be able to come up with a plan acceptable
to both Reg Fee and BOC, Sufrin said, "The problem
is that this (the tripartite funding plan) is not a
simple system. In fact, it's one of the most complicated I've ever seen."
'Somewhat confused'
Chancellor Charles E. Young, who last fall approved the switch in governance of child care from
ASUCLA to the University administration, said at a
recent press conference that he is "somewhat
confused" by the current child care situation. Young
said, "T'm very concerned about the future of child
care at this campus," and explained that he had
approved the tripartite funding concept because
"everyone convinced me this was what we should do

Now the people who convinced me are dragging
their feet."
Harlan Thompson, an assistant vice-chancellor
who is the chairman of the Child Care Advisory
Com mittee, said it is a tedious task to develop a new
budget proposal because "there is a fantastic array
of variables that are involved."
However, the committee has been able to narrow
its choices to two budgets, according to committee
member Cindy Climenson. The advisory committee
is scheduled to make a decision at its meeting next
Thursday, May 1.
*Will cost less'
Sources in the advisory committee agreed with
Thompson's assessment that the new proposal "will
cost less" than the proposal Reg Fee rejected büt
said that the savings would not be very large. The
total yearly budget is still expected to be close to
half a million dollars, the sources said.
The adivisory committee's new plans still would
divide child care into full-time and part-time centers. Currently only a full-time center is operating,
with part-time services tentatively scheduled to
begin next January, one year after an early tentative budget called for its opening.

entries.title: Funding of child care center jeopardized
entries.author: Patrick Healy
entries.text:
Funding of child care center jeopardized

By Patrick Healy and Eric Mandel
DB Staff Writers
While an advisory committee reconsiders its budget proposal, onethird of the tripartite funding plan for child care services on this campus
remains in doubt.
Under the current Child Care Center budget proposal, registration fees
have been requested to cover $62,970 of the 1975-76 budget. The rest of the
funding will come from the Associated Students (ASUCLA), state
monies, Chancellor's funds, and parents' fees. However,
Registration Fee Committee has balked on coming up with all of its
share of the funding.
Committee revises its budget proposal.
The, 10-member advisory committee, chaired by the University's
Assistant Vice-Chancellor in charge of business, Harland Thompson, has
broken into subcommittees to gather data for a cost/benefit analysis of
various child care organizations, Thompson said. The committee will
) meet again on Thursday to hegin preparing its revised presentation to
Reg Fee, which has given the committee a June 1 deadline. Thompson
expects the advisory committee to have its new proposal ready by early
next month.
Objections
Members of Reg Fee have raised several objections to the adivsory
committee's original proposal, including admissions policies, alleged
lack of a definite affirmative action program and the high cost for the
relatively few parents served. In its report to Chancellor Charles E.
Young, Reg Fee also questioned the ratios of students to faculty and staff
served by child care, noting that students are providing the bulk of the
funding through reg fees and ASUCLA money.
At Reg Fee's final meeting last quarter, administrator Winston Doby
said, "I think we've reached a consensus that the proposed plan is too
expensive."
Until this year, child care has been administered by ASUCLA:
Following a report prepared for the Chancellor by consultant Luke Fish-
- burn, the University administration has taken over control of child care:
Fishburn's report, which he described as very similar to the current
advisory committee proposal, included a recommendation that the
Child Care Center open a separate part-time center to augment the fulltime center. The part-time center would be able to serve more students.
Center capacity
Currently, the Child Care Center has a capacity for 69 full-time
children. It is caring for 74, some of whom are only at the center part-

and Thompson told the Daily Bruin they believe the Reg Fee committee
is balking at the first child care proposal because Reg Fee does not
realize how inherently expensive child care must be. "Everyene who is
not directly involved with child care is a little boggled when he first sees
the figures," Fishburn said.
UC Berkeley also operates a child care center, though all of its services are part-time. According to Susan Castro, part-time is more expensive on an hourly cost basis than full-time. She said Berkeley's
center, which is staffed entirely by professionals, cost from $2 to $2.25
per child per hour this year. Besides merely babysitting, Berkelly's
child care offers health care and educational services to the children,
Castro said.
• Berkeley's child care is divided into six centers for›different age
groups, housed in four separate facilities. The cost of running the service
includes rent on one of the facilities, and a $6,000 maintenance charge on
one of the rent -free buildings
The service can handle 143 children at one time and is presently
averaging 225 per day, Castro said
The Berkeley center is supported by registration fees, state funds and
parents' fees. Because of the state money, the Berkeley center, like the
one here, must follow several standards of service, including minimum
ratios of workers per child and a prescribed fee schedule.
An additional objeetion raised by Reg Fee to the current child care
proposal at this campus is that it does not appear fiscally sound for more
than a couple of years. In its formal recommendation to Chancellor
Young, Reg Fee stated, "The projected annual 7.5 per cent inflation cost
increase provision appears inadequate to realistically maintain the
program through 1977. The inflationary aspect of this program is antithetical to a stable state approach to Registration Fee dollar
allocations."
'Going to die'
Reg Fee member Winston Brooks said, "It seems to me it (child care
as presently outlined) is going to die."
Although the advisory committee has been asked by Reg Fee to
substantially revise its proposal, sources believe thät the committee
may only "retrench" and gather data to back up its current proposals,
making only minor changes.
Thompson said it is too early to say whether the committee will decide
to make major changes. "Anything is possible," Thompson said.
Though Thompson admitted child care could be made more
economical by cutting the ratio of workers to children to the absolute
minimum required by state law, he did not think it would be a wise
move. "I don't think the University wants to administer a desperation
Child Care Center. I know I don't want to administer one."

tne even though the reguiar part-ume center is not scheduled to be
established until next January. The current operating budget is $263,851.
The Advisory Committee's proposal for 1975-76 calls for the full-time
center to handle between 68 and 70 children, with the new part-time
center to care for an additional 74, According to Ted Eden, a member of
Reg Fee and the advisory committee, the total budget could run as high
as half a million dollars.
Besides the expanded staff necessary for the part-time center, an

Students served
Reg Fee has advocated funding the part-time center because it felt

families which could be served. Currently only 38 children of students

entries.title: Parents find Child Care Center enhances learning
entries.author: Alice Gorton
entries.text:
Parents find Child Care Center enhances learning
By Alice Gorton
DB Staff Reporter
The ASUCLA Child Care Center
sits between the tennis courts and
parking lot 1 in what used to be the
subtropical horticultural building.
Early in the morning parents
begin to carry in sleepy-eyed,
sometimes still pajama-ed little
ones. Pretty soon the area is a
natural thriving playgroundhome: infants are napping sideby-side, while the older ones take
liberty to the back yard.
Everything appears normal,
though in fact for the children it is
a rather unique experience.
Johnny Murphy, a 20-month-old
toddler, has spent half his" life
enrolled at the Child Care Center.
One of his tight buddies is lan
Battie, who at 17 months is a
veteran of almost a year at the
Center. What their parents see of
the friendship pleases them, since
they feel that lan and Johnny's is
a social experience many other
childrep never have.
Johnny's. father, Pat Murphy,

describes, his son as "very extroverted - not shy and scared
like other little kids." Cindy
-Battie, lan's mother, laughs at
her son's friendliness.
"Itake him to the grocery store;
and if he sees another child his age
he'll go up and talk - but they
don't talk back," she said.
Babysitter
Both parents know that the
experience of the Child Care
Center has enhanced the learning
and development of their
children. Without the existence of
the Center, or if they had not been
luckier than most on the waiting
list of 400 preschoolers, their
alternative would have been a
babysitter at home. "It's made a
difference in his life, and that's
what is most important," Battie
said,
Bút- aside from what these
parents see as the special
socializing advantages of the
Center, it is generally' agreed by
evervbody that problems do exist.
"The pay is so bad, and there is
DB photo by Scoft Brock

such a turnover of staff," Battie
sympathetically reports; "but the
ones who stay at the Center work
hard." The children also tend to
catch each other's colds and
viruses.
"If I had one complaint it would
be that some parents bring their
kids in sick - but after a while
the kids build up a certain immunity." Murphy concedes. He
admits that with a babysitter
there would not be this problem.
Single parents like Cindy and Pat
who are working towards their
degrees are perhaps among the
most grateful for the existence of
a child care center on campus.
Strong sense
The spirit which brought the
Center into operation three years
ago includes a strong sense of
community on the university
campus.. It is significant to note
that when higher education first
existed it was for men only. Not
just women, but married women
and mothers had to demand to be
recognized by universities. Prior
to the establishment of the
ASUCLA child care center there
was a movement for child care on
campus which included a weeklong sit-in of parents and their
small children at Ackerman
Union.
Among those active
demanding child care on campus
in 1970 were Pam and Steve Brier,
then expecting their first child.
Their daughter Jenny, now three
vears old, has been enrolled in the
Center since April of 1971.
Because -of -her parents' long
association, their view of the
Center is necessarily complex.
While Pam says that the quality of
the care is "quite-fine," she and
her husband feel that the original
vision has not been fulfilled.
Steve recalled that in 1970 approximately 2,800 students and•
employees at UCLA had
expressed a need for child care on
campus. while the Center

currently provides services for
only 131 parents. Yet in spite of the
financial and organizational
drawbacks the Center has always
faced, it has had basic advantages,
over the more expensive cost of
babysitting and over other child
care centers which only accept
children at least two years of age.
The type of family with
greatest need for child care would
in
be student or low income families
with children under two, according to general opinion.
Problems
There are operational problems
on the surface that most people
are aware of: an underpaid staff
with a high turnover rate, families
who cannot pay their bills, a long
waiting list. and a general need
for better facilities. Alison Wileox,
Child Care Center administrator,
attributes their difficulties to the
financial problems that have
plagued the center since its inception: the notion that a child
care center should be selfsupporting. Only now, according

DB photo by Scott Brock
to Wilcox, are people just
beginning to realize that such a
goal is impossible.
In its third year of operation,
partly financed by ASUCLA,
partly by fees, and at times in the
past by government grants, the
Center is presently $30,000 in debt
and only half way through the
fiscal year. Skeptical of ASUCLA
financing in the future, Wilcox
remarks. "ASUCLA is a business
and child care is not - it can't
be." She, sees the solution to
funding as'coming about only with
help from the University.
The original demands, the
demonstrations in Meyerhoff
Park, the parents and small
children who participated in the
cúlmination week-long sit-in
in Ackerman Union, and the
planned threat to bring everybody
mothers, fathers, babies,
supporters — to the Chancellor's
office for a confrontation back in
early 1971 may yet have to be
revived.

entries.title: Reg Fee says child care plan needs further study
entries.author: Tamar Manjikian
entries.text:
Reg Fee says child care plan needs further study
By Tamar Manjikian
Editor-in-Chief for a day
The Registration Fee Committee has submitted a
reaction to the child care proposal sent to Chancellor
Young on Nov. 22 by the child care study group, in
which they call for further review of five aspects of the
plan.
Stating its unanimous support for the policy of
providing child care services at UCLA, the committee
recommended the following areas of the proposal for
study:
-lack of funding for facility expansion from capital
outlay,
unrealistic estimate in the reduction of operating
expenses,
—optimistic estimate of outside funding sources,
study of the future commitments of UCLA to
child care, and
-optimistic projection for the two-year termination
date of the center.
Reg fee, which serves as an advisory body to the
Chancellor on the allocation of nearly $12 million in
student fees, advised Young that should any deficits

come about because of the number of staff members
not leaving when they are expected to, that the child
care center plan not be terminated before its scheduled
ending date - June 30, 1983.
The child care study group - composed of child
care study center staff members, parents and student
leaders - projected a savings of almost $19,000 from a
reduction of salaries and benefits expense due to staff
members leaving. Reg fee labeled this as "overly
optimistic" and thus took the position of providing
funds to offset any deficits to keep the center going
until 1983.
The committee also expressed discontent at the
Chancellor's agreement with the child care study group
to not provide funds for building projects which the
center would have to have in order to accept more
children.
A major roadblock toward the reaching of any final
agreement on child care was the high cost per child
staying at the center. Adding more toilets, for which
the capital funds were requested, would have solved
the problem to some extent by making it possible for
the center to care for more children.

The committee recommended that before the
termination date studies be done on possible increases
in university funding for the center and the
construction of a "more suitable" facility.
Reg fee also recommended to the Chancellor an
allocation of nearly $170,000 in students fees for
capital. outlay projects. The Capital Outlay Task
Force, a subgroup of the committee composed of reg
fee members and representatives from other studentdominated boards, had been given $200.000 by the
Chancellor to recommend for building projects for this
year.
The Student Health Services will receive the highest
amount of funds -if the Chancellor approves the
COTF recommendation. It has asked for nearly
$50,000 for its remodeling projects.
The committee also discussed what actions it should
take in regard to a Daily Bruin article of Feb. 21 which
members termed "inadequate" because it took the
committee members' discussion out of context. they
claimed.
Reg fee voted to request a retraction from the Bruin
and to publish an opinion column in the neuspaper.

entries.title: Child care
entries.text:
Child care
We urge Chancellor Charles E. Young to support a
proposed Child Care Center here.
The Center which would serve 200 children of students,
employees and faculty, answers to a definite need.
Due to the high costs of private child care-whether
a babysitter or a nursery school-most female students
and employees are faced with either leaving their children
uncared for, or impairing their educational or professional
lives by staying at home.
The organization and philosophy of the Child Care
Center would benefit the children as well, for it would
not be dumping ground for inconvenient offspring but
an educational opportunity for them.
In addition, the Child Care Center would provide
training in child care to underskilled and economically
disadvantaged who demonstrate ability to work well with
children; thereby benefiting not only the individual child
or trainee, but the community at large as well.
Although attempts are being made to recruit disadvantaged individuals into the University as employees
and students, there is a shortage of child care centers in
the community which seriously hampers the ability of
these individuals to accept positions as employees or to
attend the University.
There seems to be a belief on various administrative
levels that the goal of greater minority enrollment and
employment will be realized without action.
We urge Young to act, and approve the Child Care
Center: the Office of Economic Opportunity has supplied
the funds, all that is needed is Young's formal consent.

entries.title: Bill to support campus child care passes Assembly, future unsure
entries.author: Dave Peden
entries.text:
Bill to support campus child care passes Assembly, future unsure
By Dave Peden
DB Staff Writer
A bill to support on-campus child care at institutions of
higher learning throughout the State has emerged from
the California Assembly by a unanimous 62-0 vote but
apparently faces an uncertain future in the Senate and at
the hands of Governor Reagan.
The bill would tie priority of child care
services to a parent's academic workload.
According to Bond, the requests for
changes are going to be accomodated,
although "The exact language hasn't been
worked out yet."-
The measure, AB 4190, was sponsored by Assemblymen
John Vasconcellos (D-Santa Clara) and March Fong
(Alameda County) at the request of the UC Student Lobby.
The Lobby was responsible for much of the original
language in the bill.
The bill would allocate $3 million to support up to' 50
campus child care programs. Presently only 19 such
operations receive state support, including the ASUCLA
Child Care Center on campus.
Parent fees
AB 4190, in addition to direct funding of child care centers, would change the law regarding parent fees as they
are applied to State matching grants. Those child care
centers currently receiving state, monies are required to
match one-third of their State grant. For example, the
ASUCLA Child Care Center received $53,867 in State funds
and paid $17,955 back to the State.
Child care centers are presently prohibited from using
fees charged to parents to make up the matching fund.
Fees charged to parents receiving financial assistance
(welfare) must be subtracted from the State monies. The
bill would allow centers to collect their parent fees without

penalty, and would allow parent fees to be used as the
matching funds.
Revisions
The measure has undergone a series of revisions since it
was introduced the end of April. One of the most important
changes, according to Linda Bond, co-director of the
Student Lobby came at the request of Assembly members
who wanted availability of campus child care linked
directly to a student parent's course load. In other words, a
parent with a full academic course load should have a
higher priority for child care than a parent taking fewer
courses. According to Bond, the requests for changes are
going to be accommodated, although "the exact language
hasn't been worked out yet."
Governor's veto?
Throughout the bill's history, fear of veto by the
Governor has been apparent. When it was introduced, a
spokesman for Vasconcellos said, "The initial (objection
will be the amount of money. As it is now, the governor will
probably veto it."
Bond concurred with that earlier evaluation. She said,
"Governor Reagàn is acting as if Proposition 1 (a
* proposition defeated on the Juñe 4 ballot which would have
limited the State's spending) had passed. Apparently he's
trying to leave a legacy to the people of California." Bond
said "word has come down" that the Governor "will not
look favorably on new programming." Outlining plans to
get (AB) 4190 into law, Bond added, "We've got to convince
the Governor of the need to expand. The bill will get people
off of welfare and into an educational program which
eventually will get them into a permanent job."
Lost Federal funds
According to Gary Jerome of the budget division of the
State Finanee Department, there is no indieation yet of
support for AB 4190 in the State administration. Jerome
explained that the State originally began support of child
care programs to replace lost Federal funding.

entries.title: Married student housing program offers child care
entries.text:
Married student housing program offers child care
FUN AND GAMES - are encouraged at the
Parent Toddler Group nursery..
LOVE AND CARE - abound at the nursery school in the
married students housing complex.

The controversy over whether UCLA Child Care Services should
be funded with student registration fees is the most recent dispute in
the rocky seven-year history of child care services here.
In contrast to the financially plagued UCLA Child Care Services is
the Parent Toddler Group, a self-supporting child care center
located at the married student housing complex. The organization is
a co-op nursery school sponsored by the office of Dean of Students
Byron Atkinson.
The school receives University aid from Atkinson's office in the
form of rent-free space and scholarships to parents who cannot
afford the tuition, Atkinson said. No student registration fees are
used, according to his administrative secretary Beth Michaelson.
Although priority is given to residents of married student housing,
the child .care services are available to member of the UCLA
community, said director Dianne Manning.
The co-op is designed especially for parents who do not work fulltime, Manning said. The facilities can accommodate 28 children a
day, but only one session of three to four hours. Parents are also
requested to volunteer time once a week at the facilities.
Tuition is paid by parents on a sliding salary scale, ranging from
$3 to 5 an hour, which pays for the group's two professional teachers
and maintenance of the facilities. The University Child Care Service
also charges on a sliding salary scale but due to mass campus and
state subsidiès charges its users $0-1.30 per hour.
Manning said, "We're a unique place where parents can have time

entries.title: Plans approved for temporary child care center
entries.author: Joan Weinstein and John Bergstedt
entries.text:
Plans approved for temporary child care center
By Joan Weinstein
and John Bergstedt
DB Staff Writers-
Chancellor Charles E. Young, yesterday, approved the
general outlines of a plan to convert the old subtropical
horticulture building into a temporary child care center.
In a meeting last week, ASUCLA offered to act as
sponsoring organization for the child care center "from this
according to ASUCLA Executive Director
point on,"
Donald Findley.
The stipulations were that 1) it was acceptable to the
Child Care Committee established by the Chancellor last
year and the administration; 2) the duration of the experimental phase would be three years; 3) the project be as
self-supporting as possible; 4) the project serve the entire
campus community and not just the students and 5) the
administration would agree to donate temporary use of the
horticulture building for a three year period commencing
upon administration approval of a revised proposal, and
agree to pay remodeling costs.
"I am pleased that ASUCLA has volunteered to bring the
project to fruition since it is a logical ageney to respond to

this need of the campus community," Young said. "I have
every expectation that the final proposal will be acceptable
to all concerned."
Last year a number of proposals were made for a child
care center, but were frustrated by lack of money or space.
The most recent was a proposal last spring which sought
funding from the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO). It
failed because no long range commitment for space was
made.
Findley told members of an ad hoc Child Care Committee (not the same as the Chancellor's Child Care
Committee which was abolished this week) yesterday the
facilities (a total of 5,000 square feet) could accomodate
approximately 60-80 children. He added if a final proposal
submitted-by ASUCLA is accepted by the Chancellor as
anticipated, the center could begin operation as soon as
spring quarter 1971.
Members of the committee expressed approval of the
proposal: "There's no doubt in my mind that this is a
tactical victory," Sharon Heath, committee chairman said.
"It's a beautiful first step."
However, members of the committee said they must

continue to push for expanded facilities to accomodate all
children of students and employes.
Findley also said there would be some room for possible
expansion with the removal of an adjacent greenhouse to
provide space for trailers. He also said the location is "an
ideal space" because it is near the playground facilities of
the Neuropsychiatric Institute which could most likely be
used.
"We hope the proposed experimental project will
provide the first step toward determining a long range
comprehensive plan for a child care and development
center for the campus," Young said. "The proposed experimental center cannot serve all who need child care, but
we have to start somewhere."
Meanwhile, the Child Care Center Committee is planning to open a child care co-operative Monday in the
Ackerman Union Women's Lounge. The co-operative will
run from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. all through next week. Supplies
are being donated and two supervisors will be present
According to Mrs. Heath, the ratio of workers to
children is *2.5 to one at its worst, and one to one at its
best."

entries.title: In defense of Childcare
entries.author: Sally Armstrong
entries.text:
In. defense of Childcare
By Sally Armstrong
(Editor's note: Armstrong is a member of the Young Socialist
Alliance).
The future of the child care center is in doubt. Members öf the
UCLA administration who sit on the University Policies Commission,
the Registration Fee Committee, and the Campus Child Care Policy
October
Advisory Committee are spearheading an attack on the present child
care center.
The debate over child care-has been going on for five years. As
Daily Bruin writer Eric Mandel pointed out in his story of September
"The concept of on-campus child care started in 1970 with a
two and a half week 'baby-in' in the women's lounge of Ackerman
Union.",
OPINION
As a result of the publicity and support generated by this
demonstration, early in 1971 the child care center was established as
a pieocuproge er Siive the no thee ministration has attempted to
undercut the effectiveness of the center.
The key issues at the present time are to defend the existing child
care center and stop the center's foes from cutting back services and
terminating current staff members. This requires an educational
campaign to show how the administration's proposed "outreach"
program--a system of farming-out chitdren to private homes--will fail
to provide care for even as many children as the existing center.
According to Bruin writer Mandel, "outreach" advocates originally projected that between 600 and 1,200 children could be cared for
under their program. However, as Mandel points out, their most
recent report projects that by December 1976, after a year of
operation, "a minimum of 75 to 100 children will be served." This
number represents no increase in children served over the existing
center. In addition, the "outreach" program does not and cannot
guarantee high quality care.
There is general agreement among all participants in the child
care debate thät the campus center does not serve enough children.
But this fact is not the fault of the existing center, its staff, or the.
parents who have been fortunate enoughrto obtain on-campus child
care.,
The current center does not serve enough-children because it is
the victim of inadequate funding. At the root of this problem is the
fact that the resöurces of capitalist society are incorrectly allocated
Instead of-maintaining and expanding needed social services like
child care, the federal and state governments allocate funds to serve
the interests of a tiny minority of wealthy businessmen and bankers.
The sums necessary to expand social services should come from
eliminating military expenditures, raising taxes on big industry, and
placing a 100 percent tax on all income over $25,000..
The effort to abolish on-campus child care*is part of a generalized
attempt to roll back the gains.of women and oppressed minorities
such as Blacks and Chicanos. What is necessary to defend the
center is for its parents and staff to join with women's organizations,
other student, staff, and faculty groups, and concerned individuals,
to wage a massive campaign for child care through education,
rallies, picket-lines, and debates.
Sally Armstrong
biology graduate, student

entries.title: Child Care Center short of volunteers
entries.author: Steve Ainsworth
entries.text:
Child Care Center
short of volunteers
By Steve Ainsworth
DB Staff Writer
After a hectic opening three weeks ago in the subtropical horticulture
building, the ASUCLA Child Care Center here has "settled down" to the
business of caring for 85 children 10 hours every week day, according to
Betty Diamond, Child Care director.
"The children know they belong here now. They can sort of identify
with this place and it's made it a little less hectic than three weeks ago,"
Diamond said.
The children range in age from two months to five years and come from
about 120 families. The center ean accomodate 85 children at a time, but
some stay only part of the day so the center actually serves over 120
children. According to Diamond; 50 per cent of the children come from
student families, 40 per cent from employes and 10 per cent from faculty.
Volunteers
Diamond said the program is coming along very well but volunteers
and equipment are still badly needed.
Genevieve Desdevises, a student volunteer, said she felt the program
was worthwhile and rewarding. She spends three hours one day a week
working with the children.
"I think it's a great program, it's the least you can do to volunteer," she
said. A full-time staff of 15 mans the center with the help of volunteers,
but according to the Child Care Center Committee (CCCC), they have
only half the volunteers they nèed.
Horticulture building
The horticulture building was renovated in three months to allow the
Child Care Center to move there. The CCCC said the remodeling was
accomplished in the short time and within the budget because of the efforts of the Physical Plant staff under the direction of Arch O'Bryant.
Diamond said her staff is now working out the plans for a playground to
be located in a dirt field behind the horticulture building..
Diamond said many people have asked if the center could be open
evenings or weekends or if the center could expand its operation to include more children, but she said such expansion is impossible because of
the shortage of staff and equipment.
"We don't have any plans for expansion at all. We spend äll our time on
this operation," she .said.

entries.title: The Need for Child Care
entries.author: Cheryl Shaleve
entries.text:
The Need for Child Care
by Cheryl Shaleve
(Editor's note: Shaleve is a Student and has a child in the UCLA
Child Care Center).
It really isn't arguable that
child care is very expensive; no
one expected otherwise. But just
as the system of welfare in the
United States operates exhorbitantly in à never ending uphill
battle against administrations
which believe it should not and
need not exist, so the child care
OPINION
needs of the American people
are fought by many, I expect, of
like minds. Whether the administrators at federal, state, county, -child
city or university levels like it or
not, there is a need for child
care that will not diminish and
must be met. Fact: men and
women with. children work;
thousands upon thousands are
single parents. Women, especially, finding themselves alone with
children, and unskilled, must
return to schoolin order to
qualify themselves for employment. This is not a luxury. And if
the university is to function in
service to the community, these
people are among those with
the greatest need. The many
arguments have been stated often enough to have brought
child care to the university but
the administration continues to
resist.
My family is among those privileged few at the UCLA Child
Care Center. If the •center
should close down, I would be
forced to leave school. There are
others in a similar position, some
of whom are prepared to sue for
the. right to child care on this
campus. But 1 do not write for
us alone. There are hundreds of
children of students, staff and
faculty on the waiting list for
places which are all too few. I
suspect there are hundreds
more who, upon hearing that
over four hundred were already
on the list didn't even bother,
or were discouraged from even
applying. Still, the administration
would prefer a new baseball
field to any expansion of child
care, even in the face of so great
a need. •If football tickets are
shunned -at half-price specials,
why another field? What kind of
value system persists here? Is an
educated parent less important
than baseball, on campus too?
The child care center provides
420 hours a day of service to the
UCLA community, 280 hours, or
2/3, of which to the children of
students. It cannot be suggested
that Reg. Fees is wrong when it
claims too few are being served
for so much money; it is true. In

my opinion, however, the funds
should come from the university
as part of a recognized need, an
integral part of the present day
educational needs of the greater
student body, as well as a need
of faculty and staff members.
The center should not face closure, it should expand. This
campus needs child care! While
it is true that the physical plant
at UCLA leaves something to be
desired and space is limited, if a
baseball field can and is being
considered in its stead, then
there is room for expanded
child care facilities.
Beyond this, should not the
university, first in developing so
many areas of knowledge, develop our knowledge in quality
care as well? With the
growing need across the nation
and so very few experts, particularly in infant and toddler care,
isn't this an area where research
funds might contribute to furthering our knowledge and optimizing an heretofore hit and
miss experience at so vital a time
in a child's life? We have a
department of education, a department of psychology, a medical center and other related
areas which might take advantage of having such a laboratory
on campus, yet child care, a
fact of modern life though it
mày be, is fought when it might
instead contribute, when it
might be developed and its rewards shared by all.
To those of you who believe
in child care; to those of you to
whom expanded child care facilities at or through UCLA would
be a boon; to those among
students, faculty and staff alike
for whom child care is a necessity, here or off campus, I say
write, call and have your fellows
write and call the Chancellor's
office today - before the final
word comes down, and let the
administration know that we
want, need and will not acgept
an end to child care services at
UCLA. Again, it is not Registration Fees that is at fault here but
an administration that - came
kicking and screaming into child
care, to use the Chancellor's
words, and continues to oppose
it, rendering it unworkable.
We recognize that funds are
not unlimited at the university
but we also recognize that certain things are given priority
over others. We must ask the
chancellor to reject Rieg. Fees
determination and see that the
child care center is given sufficient funds to develop the kind
of program needed for the
greatest, number of children.
Such a program is already being
worked on and should not be
dismissed out of hand. The need
is too great.

Spring

entries.title: Child Care
entries.text:
Child Care
In an era of fiscal cutback programs such as the campus-child care program here are the first to be cut. This is
happening despite the fact that guaranteeing child care
helps ensure parents, particularly women, full participation in university life. For this reason child care cannot
be rejected as too expensive or impractical.
After all, can the University prove it seeks alternative
funding for child care as doggedly as it seeks funding for
defense or law enforcement related research grants?
We don't think they can, and hope the various forces in
the child care controversy will reach a short ferm
solution, extending the on-campus center till the end of
- the academic year. But the needs of campus parents will
remain unmet unless plans for a permanent center can be
realized before the expiration date.
Obviously there are shortcomings in the current set
up.Too few parents have access to the center. The
addition of a drop-in facility could partially solve this
restriction. Child care is costly. If Registration Fees end
up financing child care, the present rate of 40 per cent
student parent users is far too low. Admission to the center should be based on need, and a sliding pay scale
implemented. But the expenses should not be subsidized
by inadequate care and underpaid staff. The administrative plan for off campus care in private homes would cost
at an estimated $295 per child next year, but appears to
risk both poor care and underpaid staff.
University funding agencies must face the fact that
while child care is not kid stuff financially, neither is it a:
toy to be tossed around. Eliminating existant campus
child care will aggravate an already harmful gap in
fulfilling the needs of student parents and their children.

entries.title: UC child care centers vary; budget limits services here
entries.text:
UC child care centers vary;
budget limits services here
By Dave Peden
DB Staff Writer
The issue of child care is coming of age on this campus; according to
those most closely involved. Student government leaders - successful
*— the University Policies
unsuccessful candidates alike
Commission (UPC) and University administration are all indicating
their support for on-campus child care here.
On other UC campuses which offer child care, the situation varies
from UC Berkeley's six child care centers which serve over 300 children
of students, to UC Irvine's Center, which operates without permanent
toilets or running water, and serves only 37 children. "Child care in the
UC system is at best a touch and go situation," child care workers häve
stated
Up in the air
Here, the ASUCLA Child Care Center is apparently stilhwery much in
the air. A budget generated by an ad hoc committee which followed UPC
recommendations calling for enlargement of the center was adopted by
the ASUCLA Board of Control (BOC).
Late fast week, however, Vice Chancellor of Administration James
Hobson indicated that a second budget should be prepared and sent to
the State Department of Education to obtain a $53,867 grant to help
finance the Center. The budget calling for expansion would lose over
$200,000, the loss being made up by ASUCLA, reg fees (or another
similar source) and the Univeristy.
Since specific amounts of contributions by those various agencies had
not yet been established and the deadline for applications for state aid
was May 1, the smaller budget, with on campus funding agencies and
amounts specified, was sent to the State Department of Education
Wednesday.
New budget
The new budget, termed "a placeholder budget designed to get the
State grant," does not call for expansion and eliminates an increase of
$44,683 in staff salaries. The "placeholder" budget was sent to
Sacramento with the stipulation that it not be regarded as the final child
care budget for next year.
On other campuses, child care facilities vary greatly in size and in
terms of children served. UC Berkeley, the aforementioned giant in the
system, serves 300 children, UC Davis serves 90, UC Riverside handles
71. From there size decreases rapidly,with UC Santa Cruz taking care of
60 children, UC San Diego 46 and UC. Iryine rounding out the group with
Even more important to both parents and children who use the various
centers are the services offered. In a comparison of those services, most
centers operate throughout the University year in addition to summer.
Most of the UC facilities are coordinated with on-campus groups for
academic purposes :
The list of services offered at the various centers does not appear to be
directly correlated with the size of the Center. Berkeley and San Diego,
according to statisties compiled by workers at the UC Berkeley Center,
offer the widest range of benefits in their child care programs. Both offer
health screening for children and the services of a social worker, and UC
Berkeley offers parental education. UC San Diego offers a community
child care referral service, and is set up to handle disturbed children.
UCSD maintains the only center in the system offering such a service.

entries.title: Child care is worth students' worry
entries.text:
Child care is worth
students' worry ...
The UCLA Child Care Center is a needed facility worthy
of the financial support provided by students in the form of
registration fees. It is a vital service because, if eliminated,
most of the students with children in the facility will be
forced to leave the University, and most of these students
are women.
The Child Care Center deserves student reg fees because
argument against funding of the Child Core Ceneet ys, tht
it is a campus service which is financially supported by all
students but used by a few. But, as many of our readers
have pointed out in the past few days, this argument has
its holes.
First, the Child Care Center is not the only exception to
the rule. Much of student reg fee money is used for such
services as the Sunset Canyon Recreation Center, the Glee
Club, the Debate Club and various athletic programs here.
Surely, the same argument that has been applied to the
campus Child Care Center can also. be applied to these
student services. In addition, the elimination of the services
mentioned would not lead to a reduction in student
(mostly female) registration; the elimination of child care
would.
Secondly, just how many students have to use a service
before it is termed financially feasible? In the case of the
Child Care Center, one must look beyond the actual
number of students served to the importance of the service
provided.
The Registration Fee Committee presently allocates
$41,000 in student fees to the center. The $41,000 figure
represents about one-fifth of the center's total sources of
revenue.
It has been said, though, that if Reg Fee decides to halt
its funding, Chancellor Young will follow. Young currently
provides $27,000 to the center. Then there is the ASUCLA
Board of Control, whose members have hinted that if both
Young and Reg Fee withdraw their funds they will be
prone to follow. BOC provides matching funds of $41,000
with the Reg Fee Committee.
We hope that no matter what the Reg Fee Committee
finally decides in the way of Child Care funding, these
other fund sources refrain from following their example.
Without even making the issue an emotional one, the Child
Care Center still
seems like a sensible funding project.
