entries.title: Don't suffer, little children
entries.author: Jeff Kaye
entries.text:
Don't suffer, little children
Over one year ago, a committee to establish a free
child center at UCLA was formed. The committee
worked on several alternate proposals for such a
center, all of which were turned down by the UCLA
administration.
One such proposal was rejected by Chancellor
Charles Young even after the Office of Economic
Opportunity expressed an interest in it by agreeing to
partially fund it and by sending two representatives
out from Washington to negotiate with the administration.
A temporary child-care center has recently been
set up by the child-care center committee and will
operate until the end of the week out of the Women's
Lounge in the student union building. The facilities
there are obviously inadequate although the committee is managing to take care of about 30 children a
day.
But 30 children of campus workers and students
out of an estimated 2,800 children who need day care
(the figures, incidentally, are taken from a 1969 poll
which didn't include children of workers in the med
center) is just not sufficient especially when even the
limited facilities in the Women's Lounge will not be
available after this week.
Needs
Although the administration has agreed to consider a plan to convert the old subtropical horticulture building into a temporary child care center,
even this plan would not adequately meet the needs
of the people involved. First of alll, the building would
not be able to accomodate more than 75 children.
Also, if the plan goes into effect, it won't start
operating until April 1971._
Furthermore, the center would be under the aegis
of Donald Findley of ASUCLA (the same man who
finds it perfectly reasonable to pay his workers no
more than $3,000 per year, while, he, himself, goes
home with about $25,000 for the same time period -
not because he works harder) instead of being
controlled in a cooperative fashion.
In a society where the needs of people are
paramount motivating factors, child-care centers
would be inevitable phenomena. In ours, child-care
centers are institutions that have to be begged for.
Child-care centers are not places for the encouragement of overpopulation, as someone foolishly
suggested in a recent letter to the Daily Bruin, but
are places in which basic human needs are met.
It is inhuman, both for the parents and for the
child, to prevent parents who are already in dire
financial straits from obtaining jobs simply because
no child care is available for their children.
Another important factor is the effect that child

-By Jeff Kaye
care centers have on women. In a society where the
care of children is almost always relegated to
women, thereby preventing many of them from
acquiring jobs and functioning in other capacities,
child care centers can be actual liberating institutions for women who see themselves only in
terms of their men, their housework and their childraising.
Arguments against the establishment of a childcare center are not very convincing. One DB reader
suggested that it would be just as preposterous to
have a child care center as it would be to have an old
Car Care Center.
I would not like to be that reader's child! The
equation of children with automobiles may stand up
in a logic class, but, in human terms, that argument
is frightening. The same reader goes on to suggest
that "shifting responsibility for children to people
other than parents" is, in some way, "illogical."
This reader's sense of logic escapes me.
I prefer to speak more in human terms, and thus I
consider it both logical and humane to argue that if a
person needs help, he should be helped, regardless of
archaic social mores.
Water
To argue against child care centers merely on
financial grounds is another position that doesn't
hold much water. Reagan cuts welfare budgets on
the same premise. Putting financial costs above
human needs is a policy which happens to be an intrinsic part of the system under which we live that I
cannot go along with.
Another argument, already referred to in this
column, against child care centers is that these sorts
of institutions encourage people to have more
children. The poverty of this line of argument is
evident when one realizes that without adequate
child care, children are penalized for being born.
This might, of course, beneficially effect the problem
of overpopulation, but that is not to say that we
should adopt every solution that might have a
beneficial effect on that problem.
Genocide, for instance, would help immeasurably
(and our government is already practicing that
solution to a certain extent), but I would not favor it.
If actions we take are detrimental to the welfare of
people, then those actions should be seriously
questioned.
In all, a child care center (that should, one day, be
free of charge) is an answer to many of the problems
that confront us, especially insofar as women are
concerned.
It seems that we should be motivated by ope
important factor in this issue and all other issues -
that is, an overriding sense of humanity.

Adopts requested budget but reduces allocation by 10 percent

the University Registration Fee

entries.title: Severe child care shortage: Program here finds sitters
entries.author: Tammy Bedrosian
entries.text:
Severe child care shortage:
Program here finds sitters
By Tammy Bedrosian
Seventy children who spend their days on campus have some
competition; more than 500 other kids want their spaces in the
Child Day Care Center.
Actually, the parents of the children on the waiting list are the
anxious ones. To alleviate that anxiety, the center has established
a Child Care Outreach Service to meet the immediate needs of
UCLA students, faculty and staff.
The free program helps at least 25 parents a month find care for
their children. "It's a hard shopping trip for parents; there is no
short cut. People need to feel there is someone to stick with them
through the process, not just give them a few names," Outreach
Coordinator Judy Bencivengo said.
"The first part of the service," Bencivengo said, "is to educate
the parents to the importance of making a careful selection in
child care so that they choose a plan that matches their values and
supplements the care they are able to provide for their families.
"These are the formative years for the child's ability to learn
and function in life, so you cannot just choose a babysitter."
The average UCLA family seeking child day care consists of
two parents, one attending school and the other working,
Bencivengo said. The biggest demand in child care is for infants
less than 6 months old, she added.
Because parents, especially mothers, experience a lot of anxiety
over leaving their child with someone during the day, the
program's weekly forums discuss guilt about leaving the child
with a stranger and the parents' concern that they will be replaced
Continued on Page 11

Child care
Continued from Page 10
by the caregiver.
"It's amazing that, through
conversation, people's anxiety
level can be quelled," Bencivengo said.
Most of the education of
parents takes place in a Child
Care Information Forum, at
noon every Monday in the
Women's, Resource Center,
Dodd 2.
"This forum gives them
1nformation about +hings to consider before making a choice,
what to pay, and supplies them
with several resources to
explore," Bencivengo said
Parents learn about the options
of sending their child to a
family day care home
licensed to care for up to six
children — or other child care
center, or hiring someone to
care for the child in his own
home.

They learn to set guidelines
for the child's eating, sleeping
and toilet instructions, - and
about the child's need for activities and stimulation. The business aspects of the child care
arrangement and a plan for
parent involvement are also
diseussed.
The Child Care Outreach
Service was started a year ago
with funds: from Dart Industries (makers of Tupperware) as a demonstration of
how employers could meet
employees' child care needs. By
setting up a network of day
care homes, the center has
found care for 250 children
under the program, Bencivengo said.
The UCLA Child Day Care
Center charges $330 a month
for infants and toddlers and

7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
weekdays.

entries.title: BOC funding vote: it's time to Care
entries.text:
BOC funding vote:
it's time to Care
The UCLA Child Care Center, a needed facility for parents
who double as students, is once again threatened with
extinction. Today, the Board of Control will consider
eliminating ASUCLA funding of the center.
This center performs a vital service because, if eliminated,
most of the students with children in the facility will be
forced to withdraw from the University.
An argument used by opponents of the center is that
spending over $40,000 to help fund the center, which they
claim benefits less than 100 students, is an unfair use of
studént funds. But judging from the response of our readers
and the large turnout at the last Reg Fee meeting, where a
similar motion was defeated, this argument has its holes.
The BOC report, compiled by members Robert David, Art
Cabral and Richard Tricker, fails to respond to the issue of
whether the campus either needs or should pay for an oncampus child care center. Nor does the report give*
suggestions on alternate sources of income for the center,
should BOC decide to stop its funding.
In addition, many BOC members claim they are not against
the Child Care Center, but rather against ASUCLA funding of
the center. This is a ridiculous statement since these members
know if they vote to cut off funding, it is very likely that the
Reg Fee Committee and Chancellor Charles Young will follow
suit, thus bringing an end to the center.
The absence of solutions to their argument show the
carelessness in which this report is founded. We hope the rest
of the Board of Control acts in a more responsible manner and
votes to continue to fund this vital service to students.

entries.title: Child care should be supported
entries.author: Martin A. Rothblatt
entries.text:
Child care should be supported
The ASUCLA Board of Control
(BOC) meets this Friday to vote
on its 1978-79 contribution to our
Child Care Center. ASUCLA is a
non-profit student organization
which runs every store, vending
machine and food facility on
campus. They take in a lot of
money. Thanks in large part to
non-student general manager
Don Finley, they've made profits
for the past several years. BOC
decides how to spend these
profits.
Historically, the Board has sought to develop allocation plans which balance three basic
needs: 1. the need to invest in long-term development of its facilities and services, 2. the
need to reinvest portions of. available net revenues in working capital in order to
maintain the financial health of the Association, and 3. the need to serve immediate
needs of its student membership and the campus community at large, through such
programs as the Spring Bonus Program, Child Care support, and so forth.
Board of Control policy for the allocation of available net revenues, 1977
Child Care Center exists primarily to allow students with
young children to attend UCLA.
Beyond that, the Center is a
model for society. The Center
shows that having a child does
not automatically send a
woman into the twilight zone of
toilet bowl marinas, truncated
opportunities and stereotypic
fulfillment. The Center shows
women may avoid a housewife
role without being guilt-ridden
that her child is in the mindnumbing environment characteristic of so many profit-making offcampus child care centers.
Opportunity for advancement
is possible for many UCLA
students only because UCLA has
a Child Care Center. The many
departments which use the
Center, and the visitors it has
attracted from countries around
the world, attest to the high
quality of services offered.
(Editor's Note: Rothblatt is a
student attending law school
here.)

By Martin A. Rothblatt
OPINION
We all stand to gain from the
contributions to society that will
be made by women with dreams
and goals beyond those of being
a good mother. The energies of
those women, if not quashed by
the closing of Centers like ours,
may very well help to clean the
air, increase crop yields, or
humanize government policies.
We all stand to gain from the
future contributions of children
brought up in a warm and
stimulating environment staffed
by caring and responsive professionals. It is to children like those
in our Center that we entrust the
responsibility of solving the
problems we will have missed or •
have created. Thus the Child Care
issue is not solely a woman's or a
parent's issue. It deeply concerns
us all.
This- year, BOC is composed
entirely of men. Some members
are concerned that the Child
Care Center is not generating
profits of its own. Dividends from
truly worthwhile investments are
often long in coming and rarely
calculable in pecuniary terms.
(The output of the two year olds,
though impressive, has few
markets beyond their parentsl).
Most major corporations now
realize their social responsibilities
and allocate a percentage of

profits to various public problems. ASUCLA, which makes its
profit off the tools of enlightenment and the sustenance of those
getting enlightened, must also
show responsibility to its community. This can admirably be
accomplished by continuing its
present level of financial support
for the Child Care Center.
The student's choice is clear.
Two weeks ago, faced with
overwhelming student support,
the Reg Fee Committee voted
down a proposal to eliminate the
Center.
BOC is to be applauded for
their past support. It is hoped that
the elimination of women from
the committee will not alter
BOC's historical committment to
the Center. As BOC's own "Policy
for the Allocation of Available
Net Revenues" says, Child Care is
an "immediate need of its
student membership and the
campus community at large."
So that students with children
may continue their education,
urge all to come to BOC's
meeting and support the Child
Care Center. So that women may
begin to get a shot at opportúnities long denied them, please
attend, at 1 PM, Friday April 21, in
the large lounge on the second
floor of Ackerman Union. So that
our children and our future will
be bright, let's fill the meeting
room with men and women for
fairness, students for corporate
responsibility, people for a better
tomorrow.

entries.title: A fight for expanded child care
entries.author: Pam Brier
entries.text:
A fight for expanded child care
by Pam Brier
(Editor's note: Brier is a member-of the Campus
Committee for Child- Care). dent David Saxon's words,
The Committee for Campus Child Care is a
group of UCLA students, faculty and staff, both
parents and non-parents, whose purpose is to
build a broad-based movement to fight for the
continuation and expánsion of part-time and full-
OPINION
time child care at UCLA. At least 3000 families
have expressed a need for child care here.
-It is the responsibility of the university's administration to support child care by providing facilities
and money. The proposed " ouitreach program"
will not provide acceptable child care, but onlys
glorified referral service for babysitting throughout West L.A. and operated by persons who witl
be paid only $255/month to care for four children
full-time. Only on-campus child care can insure
parents' access to the program and their participation in its planning and the daily care of their
children.
The administration's attack an the child care
program at UCLA is but one part of a larger,
attack on working conditions, student programs
like ethnic studies, special admissions and
financial aid, and social services such as health
care. Because of its continuing stagnation U.S
capitalism has stepped up its attacks on working
"people through wage cuts, speed-ups and layoffs
and has reduced its demand for college-educated
people. Asrecent Dept. of Laborpamphlet,
"Occupational Manpower and Training Needs"
contends that there are one million more students than the economy needs and that the
,numbers by the early 1980s. The cutbacks at
UCLA and throughout the country are the
universities' way to reduce the number of stu-

dents and to generate profits by, in U.C. Presi-
"pruning down, phasing out" vital programs.
While the needed money for on-campus child
care is available, it's allocated instead for projects
like the ASUCLA student store expansion, north
campus student union and restaurant, and the
Alumni Center. These projects have nothing to do
with the quality of education and do not meet
the basic needs of students, staff and faculty. They
.are designed, on the one hand, to make profit for
the university, and, on the other, to develop it as
an elitist institution which is effectively closed to
poor, working and -minority people. That is why
we must fight all these attacks as students and
workers are doing across the country.
The Committee for Campus Child Care demands on-campus child care facilities which: (1)
can serve all students, faculty and staff who need
them; (2) provide, care for children of ages 2
months through*5 years; (3) are located at several
sites on campus; (4) include a full--and part-time
center and a drop-in center (night shift); (5) are
backed by long-term financial guarantee from
tunding sources to insure stability.. Ironically,
these.demands are almost identical to those published in the Bruin by the UCLA Child Care
Center Committee in 1970 and which resulted in

however small and limited. Since that time, people associated with the existing child care facility
and other supporters of child care have demanded expanded facilities appropriate to the divergent needs of the campus parent community. We
need to link our struggles at UCLA to the struggles for child care at other university campuses
and in society at large. We need to resist efforts
to set parents aginst non-parents, men against
women, students, faculty and staff against® each
other, and parents against children. We urge you
to support this struggle.

entries.title: Child care center gets new director
entries.author: Nancy Gottesman
entries.text:
Child care center
gets new director
By Nancy Gottesman
Staff Writer
"I applied for the job not because I was crazy or a masochist, but
pecause I like this type of work, the kids and the parents," said June
Sale, the new Child Care Services director.
Sale became director on Feb. 1 after working as a consultant
ince September to try and help save the child care program, which
vas having funding problems.
"We've got a tremendously dedicated staff whose energy had
een sort of sapped by all the problems here. But, we are definitely
n existence. We're alive and well and we've got a lot to do."
Foremost among those things they have "got to do" is Sale's plan
o develop a health program for the service's 67 children, who range
n age from 2 months to 6 years.
In addition to health care programs, Sale plans to implement
program trying to involve volunteers with UCLA Child Care
ervices.
"Day care is expensive and we've had a very big cutback in staff.
major part of the expense is salary for staff and teachers; one
dult is needed for every four children under 2.9 years (of age)."
Sale said she is going to try to establish joint programs with
cademic departments, such as social welfare and public health, in
rder to obtain some of their volunteers.
"We're also going to go to some older and retired people in the
ommunity and see if they'd like to come volunteer," she said. "And
e'd love to get high school and UCLA students here."
As a result of the cutback in funds that child care has
sperienced, Sale said the program must develop its own fundising events to make up for their monetary losses.
"We're going to try to have a self-supporting center. We will be
ole to operate on state funding and our fund-raising programs,
ut we're not going to rely on outside campus funds or the
" Sale said.
nancellor anymore,
A food program and grant proposals are also being planned for
e center, Sale said. But she declined to comment when asked
pout any other plans.
"I'm reluctant to say at this point. But we are going to make this
ne best day care program on the West Side," she said confidently.

entries.title: Temporary child center established in dormitory
entries.text:
Temporary child center
established in dormitory
A temporary child care center will be established for two
weeks, beginning this Monday, in the ping-pong-lounge of Hedrick
Hall.
The action was approved last night by the' Hedrick Hall
Assembly, after meeting with the Child Care Center Committee
and Commissioner of Student Facilities, Matt Mazer.
However, according to Hedrick Hall President Mike Kaplan,
the assembly in a vote of 5 to 4 decided to reconsider their action
following the initial approval of the plan.
Pressure
"Several representatives (one from each floor in the dorm) felt
they were pressured into voting ..," Kaplan said.
The trial child care center now operating in the Ackerman
Union Women's Lounge will be forced to move tomorrow and according to Mazer, the center will fold if Hedrick Hall does not allow
the use of its facilities.
Final determination of the center's location in Hedrick will be
made by the dorm residents who will be polled on retaining the
center after one week of its operation.
Distraction
If a majority of the students feel the center is distracting or an
inconvenience, it will be forced to re-locate. Should the residents
decide to retain the center in its ping-pong lounge, it will probably
remain there through Winter Quarter and until permanent quar::
ters can be established.
Two weeks ago Chancellor Charles E. Young approved the
general outlines of a plan to convert the old subtropical horniculture building into a child care center, however adjustments
must be made before it can accomodate the children.
Kaplan said a petition opposing the center's establishment in
Hedrick Hall was circulated before last night's meeting and
received 54 signatures. He said it represented floor officers, three
members of his cabinet and several house advisors.
The dorm is a place for residents and they should be allowed
access to any given recreation room," he said. However, he added
if the residents support the center, it will remain in the dorm.
Mazer, who is posting a $500 bond for any damage, "that
probably won't occur," said he hoped Hedrick's residents would
realize approving the center was an avenue for involvement and a
worthwhile way to serve the University.
Jack Kropf, manager of the auxiliary and service enterprises,
which includes the residents halls, said Hedrick's assembly showed
"good leadership in giving the center a fair trial."

entries.title: Reg Fee cuts to WRC, child care ruled final
entries.author: Chris Cameron
entries.text:
Reg Fee cuts to WRC,
child care ruled final
By Chris Cameron
Senior Staff Writer
Registration Fee Committee members stood
firm Wednesday on their decisions to cut funding
to Child Card services by half and to eliminate
funding. for the Women's Resource Center,
despite the last-minute appeals by supporters of
both groups.
Reg Fee Chair Diana Shepherd said that the
committee had passed the stage during which
reconsiderations of budget recommendations
could be raised. She said the committee, as of this
week was closed to moves to alter funding level
figures for next year.
The committee will meet with Chancellor
Young in mid-June to discuss the more than $10
million in reg fee appropriations it has proposed
over the last seven weeks. According to Reg Fee
officials, the recommendations have been
compiled and are scheduled to go to the printer
today
During the course of Wednesday's meeting, a
number of Reg Fee members and representatives
of the Women's Resource Center protested the
drastic cuts in both WRC and Child Care.
Administration representative Tony Sypinski,
who fought the Child Care resolution when it was
introduced by undergraduate Debbie Hammond®
two weeks ago, was again critical of the cut.
He exptained that the committee's rush to
forward its recommendations to the printer for
publication could be standing in the way of an
intelligent decision on the heated child care issue.
"The whole history of the committee this year
has been one of deadlines broken," he said. "Why
should we bust our asses now?"!
Child Care was one of the first service areas
reviewed by the committee this year. After leaning
strongly toward cutting off funding to the center,
the committee - under pressure from over 100
Child Care supporters in a packed meeting room
- voted for a 10-percent reduction.
But two weeks ago, that allocation, which
totalled just over $37,000, was cut to about
$18,000. Child Care officials were ordered by the
committee to expand an off-campus family-home
day care program, and to charge fees to parents
of children using the service. The student parents,
the committee added, would be eligible for
financial assistance from the financial aid
department here.
Child Care supporters, however, say that the

Diana Shepherd
service stands to lose its $67,000 state grant if it
charges standard fees. State regulations now
forbid child care facilities receiving grants to
charge fees other than the nominal fees
established by law on a special scale,
When other members of the committee -
including Administration rep Betty Thomasquestioned the end of funding to the Women's
Center, Reg Fee officials remained unswerving.
Debbie Hammond, who supported the
elimination, declared that the WRC funds. were
cut because UCLA women could find the services
the center provides at a host of other departments
receiving reg fees.
According to Hammond, the Placement and
Career Planning Center, Psychological Counseling, and Program Task Force were just a few of
the reg fee-supported services duplicating WRC
duties.
The Women's Genter, in addition to referring
women to community and campus agencies who
provide services ranging from assertion training
to self-defense, sponsors a variety of seminars on
career planning, lesbianism, and other women's
issues

entries.title: Child Care

entries.title: Child Care Center here progresses toward future in spirit of chary optimism
entries.author: F. R. Serrano
entries.text:
Child Care Center here:
progresses toward future
in spirit of chary optimism
By P.R. Serrane
DB Staff Writer
On a warm winter day in Westwood, the children
frolicked in their sunny playground. Boys and girls of
pre-school age clambered over a jungle gym. An
inventive, bright-faced boy named Keith took the
aluminum ladder that had been hanging on a low
rung of the framework and placed it securely higher
up. The young teacher said she had never seen that
done before, and approved. Trust it to the kids.
Other children played on swings or hobbyhorses, or
elsewhere in that crowded yard that appeared to be
in constant motion. Toddlers, barely old enough to
walk, made sand castles in the cool shade of palm
thatch; young men and women looked on, supervising, participating, helping
Constructive
Far removed from the constant commotion of
Westwood Boulevard, it. was playtime at the
ASUCLA Child Care Center. The facility is now
nearing the end of its second year at its site behind
the Credit Union on south campus, across from the
medical center. Those past two years have been
encouraging, constructive ones for the center. Its
director, Nancy Lewis, looks forward to the future
with cautious optimism.
"This place is a struggling organization," Lewis,
head of the operation since December 1971, said.
"You're at the grass roots, and building." But Lewis
thought much progress had been
made
strengthening the facility. "I've seen something
that's disorganized pulled together,", she said.
Applications
There are now 95 children on the center's roll. The
figure includes part-timers. Lack of space in the
present building dictates the limitation, and 300
applications on the waiting list are ready to take up
any slack that might appear.
There is no room to take care of those with temporary or unpredieted needs. "We've, got too many.
children now," Lewis said. "People come here with
emergencies — a man's wife has died, or a mother
has to go into the hospital - we have to tell them that
there is no way we can take care of their child."
Building
That building south of the tennis courts which now
houses the Child Care Center used to be part of the
old botany department. Inside, the children are
divided into four groups by age: infants, 2 months to
a year; toddlers, 1 to 2 years; run-abouts, 2 to 3,1/2
years; and prescheolers, 3 1/2 to 5 years.
The number of groups is neatly demanded by the
layout of the physical structure of the center; there
are only four large rooms available for classrooms.
Some of the divisions are too large, Lewis said,
placing children of very different ages together. If
space permitted, the center would organize around a

greater number of groups, each tailored to the need
and interests of a particular age.
In one of the classrooms, a sign hanging from th
ceiling proclaimed "The Thinking Corner." Artworl
decorated the walls; near the entrance, a row of little
lockers was labeled with children's names. Hanging
on the wall, a row of adult-sized toothbrushes was
similarly tagged.
A number of paper cups miniature flowerpots -
sat in the window awaiting the germination of the
contents. I know it was a window, because that
what it said underneath, in letters 3 inches tall
"w-i-n-d-o-w." On the phonograph is a disc from
Panda Records, titled "A Black-Eyed Monkey
Named Bunkey." This, like the other teacher')
materials, is placed conveniently, on a shelf, out d
reach.
Within the limited resources of the facility, space
are allotted on the basis of parents' needs and certaif
considerations of balance. "We try to have
heterogeneous climate :
cultural, economic and
racial," Lewis said. "We always try to keep a socia
ánd racial balance," she said, stating that - the
desired racial balance had been achieved in all age
groups except the oldest.
Parents' needs are judged on the basis of-prioriti
groupings; the highest priority IS. assigned H
children of single
parents. Successively
priorities are given to students' children, student
in staff pairings, children of two university employees
and families in which one spouse is not connectel
with the university.
At the center now, however, the number
children of single parents is limited to, about 30 pel
cent. "We don't want much more-than that," Lewi
said, although she stated that the center could juss
about fill the places available with children from tha
eategory if that was the object.
Emphasis *
With the emphasis on serving students; the cente.
is planning to allocate 60 per cent of its spaces t
students' children. The majority of the rest of thi
spaces currently ge te children of non-academio
employees, although faculty members too
eligible.
A little more than half the cost of operating the
center — $150,000 per year. comes from parents
fees. "They are too high," Lewis said, "but they
don't begin to cover thè expense.
"It is impossible to have child care that wilk pay for
itself," Lewis said -families that can afford to pay
the cost can afford to have babysitters. The centen
now distributes $12,000 worth of partial scholarshig
aid to the especially needy; "we don't want to turn i
into a poor ghetto," she said, adding, "but we want to
serve poor people because they need it the most,
she added.

→ "The biggest expense in child care is salaries." At
the center, parents are encouraged to help volunteer
their time to work with the children, and they are
given the incentive of a reduction in fees. Parents are
urgently needed to help elean the center in the
lower evenings as well; "we need floors to be scrubbed and
rugs to be shampooed every night," Lewis emphasized.
But notwithstanding the welcome volunteer help,
Lewis added, "We don't want to lose our parents
working; they can learn what's going on with their
children, they can learn to be better parents. Parents
working here with their children is one of the richest
things we have in child care."
Volunteer help
Volinteer help of all kinds, in fact, makes up the
major portion of the center's staff. There are about
30 student volunteers. "The students add a lot of life
energy * they roughhouse with the older kids,'
Lewis said.
Although classroom space at the Child Care Center
are - is crowded, the available outdoor play area is even
more limited. The playground immediately adjacent
to the center is small, so children are taken across
Westwood Boulevard to the Neuropsychiatric In-.
stitute playground. "There are trees to climb,"
Lewis said, "we couldn't live without it."
Space, costs
There is no desire, however, to expand the present
facility. "We need more places like this, set up in
different spots around campus," Lewis said. "We
should never have any more child eare eenters
larger than this one," she added.
Sickbay needed
Présently, Lewis said, one most pressing need is a

sickbay, for children who become ill - along with a
nurse. A larger professional staff is also desired.
It is hoped that these, and other• immediate
necessities, will be funded by a $55,000 grant for
which the center has applied.
Uncertain
The under which the Chancellor
agreement
founded the Child _Care Center two years ago was
that the operation must be self-supporting, Lewis
explained. "ASUCLA has given us tremendous
support," Lewis said, but the Center has incurred a
great deal of debt.
The grant would relieve the precarious financial
position in which the center now operates "if we
got all the money,". Lewis warned. "It's very uncertain how much money we're going, to get," Lewis
said. "It's very shaky; wé don't know how long it will
be for and we haven't received a penny of it yet."
At this point, however, the experiment with the
center has been such an outstanding and continued
success that it is doubted whether the operation
would be allowed to flounder for merely financial
reasons. For the organization has seemed to fulfill
that ideal stated some time ago by the ASUCLA
Child Care Center's first director, Betty Dimond:
"Our goal is to create and maintain an environment, both relational and physical, which says
'be' to little children and their families . where
potential in every part of human need —social, intellectual, physical, emotional can have a chance
for fulfillment. For then comes the confidence of
oneself as a worthwhile, self-affirming, competent,
person able to cope with life, and to be
responsible to self and ,to others, living life effectively and joyously.".

entries.title: Time to Compromise
entries.text:
Time to Compromise
The future of the Child Care Center here
is in jeopardy again. The Registration Fee
Committée, one of three campus funding DAY CARE CENTER
sources, has rejected the Child Care
Advisory Committee's latest proposal to CLOSED
impiement an expanded program here. The
Registration Fee Committee said the plan
costs.too much for the number of people it
serves.
Registration Fee's action makes it clear
that the controversy has become a war of
experts. Experts on budgets and budget
trimming justifiably concerned with the
best possible allocation of funds make up
one side. Their opponents are experts
determined to provide the university
community with the best possible Child
care service.
Obviously, this is not a new problem. All
budgets and all programs are. compromises LCD
between the practical and the optimum.
This controversy, however, is older and

more complex. It has been going on for
five years.
Any child care program agreed to can pe
expanded when the University is able to
find the funds. Pushing for the optimum,.
however, may well result in a total cutback
of all such programs, which would not be
to the benefit of parents or children. The
agreement and the basic program are the
necessity.
Child care is supplementary to the.
university program and must be regarded
so. In an era of tight budgets those
functions of the University least essential to
the task of educating adults must be cut
back. We need to have a Child Care Center
here, but we need one that is logical
compromise reflecting the basic requirements of small children away from home,
and fiscal responsibility on the part of the
university. The ball has been rolling long
enough. Let's compromise.

entries.title: UPC focuses upon child care conflict
entries.author: Leone Cherksey
entries.text:
UPC focuses upon
child care conflict
By Leone Cherksey
DB Staff Writer
Differences between the UPC's May 1974 Child
Care report and the report by Luke Fishburn,
chairman of the Child. Care Steering Committee,
dominated discussion at last Friday's University
Policies Commission (UPC) meeting.
UPC passed a resolution requesting the steering
committee meet and evaluate Fishburn's report, as
Don Hartsock, UPC representative to the committee, reported that only individual evaluations by
other members were made. According to UPC
members, the Fishburn report overstepped its
function by making policy recommendations instead of only discussing implementation of policies
already suggested by UPC.
According to Hartsock, key differences are: the
UPC report emphasizes the relationship between
academic research and child care - whereas Fishburn's report insists on service to parents as child
care's major aspect - and the governance issue.
The UPC recommendations clearly state the child
care center shall be administered by the University, whereas, according to Hartsock, Fishburn
leaves the question open by saying the University
can contract this work out to ASUCLA.
Anne Lawrence, UPC executive officer, said she
felt UPC's statement that the Child Care Center
should continue to be supported by ASUCLA was
being "misused" to justify the possibility of
ASUCLA governance of the Center.
UPC chairman Alan Katz claimed the Chan--
cellor's option would be to accept the UPC report for

its general policy and glean from Fishburn's report
implementation details: Asked by Lawrence what
the "tone" to the Chancellor would be, Katz said it
would be that "the report on the. whole did not
receive the proper response," that the UPC wished
a written response.
Glenn Graves a faculty representative to UPC,
objected that a more formal relationship between
UPC and the Chancellor would become, "more
antagonistic, more political," and said "He
(Young) may decide to hell with the whole UPC".
Katz responded he might decide to do that anyway
"but let us meet every two weeks."
A resolution was introduced calling for 3,750 out of
4,000 square feet allocated by Young (from private
gift funds) to expand the Faculty Center to be
reallocated a drop-in child care center. The
resolution was tabled for "further investigation"
into its feasibility. Katz said after the meeting the
motion had been intended and received in a
humorous vein. However, Stu Needman, student
representative who made the motion, said he had
intended it seriously.
In other business, a tentative plan was reached
for a University-wide governance conference in late
January, and Dean Byron H. Atkinson made a
progress report on low-cost student housing.
Don Hartsock made four separate suggestions for
setting up the conference. A mixture of three of
them was settled on for further committee work.
The mixture combined soliciting campus community input through the Bruin, holding prehearings this fall to determine the agenda and guest
list, and holding the conference in January.

entries.title: Child care control to move to Murphy
entries.author: Leone Cherksey
entries.text:
Child care control to move to Murphy

By Leone Cherksey
DB Staff Writer
Chancellor Charles E. Young announced plans to transfer the ASUCLA
Child Care Center to the office of
James W. Hobson, Vice Chancellor-
Administration, in a letter to the
University Policies Commission
(UPC) last Friday.
The letter was in response to UPC's
request for a formal answer from
Young to the UPC Child Care report
issued last May.
Young announced five decisions
which basically follow recommendations by child care consultant Luke
Fishburn, who was hired last summer -
following UPC's request to do an indepth study of child care on campus.
He submitted his report in September.
Young's decisions are:
the transfer of the Center from
ASUCLA to the Vice-Chancellor-
Administration "as quickly as is
feasible,"
- "an immediate study" of site and
funding feasibility for a part-time
Center to begin spring quarter 1975 (in
addition to the full-time center),
budgeting and funding of the
Centers to follow Fishburn's

entries.title: SLC allocates minority funds
entries.author: Ken Peterson
entries.text:
• deticit
Free child care causes
SLC allocates minority funds

By Ken Peterson
DB Staff Writer
Student Legislative Council (SLC) approved the
use of $8250 for minority student scholarships to the
ASUCLA child care center. The funds, approved
Wednesday, come from the $1 ASUCLA activity fee
approved by the student body in 1969,
According to Pam Briar, one of the parents on the
governing board of the child care center, scholarship
funding is presently running at a deficit and the SLC
funds were needed in order to take on more parents
• who need the service.
"We're trying to take on people from the waiting
list, but we can't without more scholarship money"
Briar told SLC.
LaMar Lyons, community service commissioner,
voiced his apprehension that the money might be
taken from one area where the funding was needed in
order to bolster the child care scholarship program.
He also questioned the structure of the present
program as opposed to the original child care plan
drawn up in 1969.
Betty Diamond, director of the center, explained
the present program differs only in that free child
care could not be provided and the center is not as
large as originally anticipated.
"We have projected an expansion of the center, but
right now we don't have the money. This is also the
reason the center isn't free," Diamond said.
Bill Winslow, a general representative, said the
committee formed to allocate the funds had found no
better idea than the plan to give some of the monies
to the child care center.

"We have the responsibility to allocate the funds in
some direction and I believe this plan to be acceptable," Winslow said.
SLC also voted to sponsor in principle a petition by
the American Federation of State, County, and
Municipal Employes union urging an end to cutbacks
in Gov. Ronald Reagan's 1971-72 state budget.
,The petition urges the State legislature to abolish
tuition, end the wage and hiring freeze, stop layoffs
of State employes, fund fully Educational Opportunities Program (EOP) and other special
programs for minority students, and recognize
public employes' unions as collective bargaining
agencies.
The petition also states its signers will urge increased taxation of banks, large corporations, and
agri-businesses, higher taxes on profits, and taxes on
mineral wealth being taken out of California.
The union also plans a rally in Sacramento on May
15 to protest the budget cuts.
*SLC also approved the use of the undergraduate
student association emblem on a plaque to be given
to Mae West when she visits this campus next
Wednesday night to receive an award as "Woman of
the Century." She will appear under the auspices of
the Asociated Students' Speakers Program.
In other action, Bob Cohen was approved as the
successor to Bob Elias as head of the speakers
program for next year. Cohen has been working with
the program this past year and is also involved with
UCLA-TV.

entries.title: UC student lobby wins major victory
entries.author: Dave McNary
entries.text:
UC student lobby wins 'major victory
By Dave McNary
DB Staff Writer
The UC Student lobby has already won a major victory in
the State Legislature, according to the Associated Students
Legislative Counsel, Richard Twohy.
He said the student lobby had worked to kill a bill in
committee that would make it easier for the University to
revoke a student's financial aid if he has been involved in a
eampus disturbance.
Twohy was hired by the Associated Students two months
ago to establish the student lobby in Sacramento in order to
tell the Legislature about student concerns.
Regents
He said the lobby had also helped the education committee approve the two other bills: onè to have the Regents
increase women's enrollement in UC graduate schools and
another which pressures the Regents to support child-care
centers on each campus.
"Killing the first bill was a real victory, because the bill
was quite oppresive," Twohy said. The bill would have
eliminated the provision specifying a special hearing board
be convened to consider suspension of state scholarships of
a student involved in misconduct at a University. Thus, the
Administration would have the decision.
Twohy said, "Our argument to committee members was
not one about due process. Rather, we opposed it because
the particular penalty is inherently discriminatory to the

poor, as they are the ones recetving státe assistance."
Punishment
"We felt this punishment should remain as difficult to
enforce as the law now allows."
He also argued that most of the available sanctions (such
as probation, suspension, prohibition from campus activities) seem appropriate as penalties for destructive acts,
and the University should be able to use these, rather than
suspension of financial aid, without hearings or needless
delay.
Twohy added, "Because of the special inequity of this
punishment. it seems unjust that administrators should
have access to it at all.".
The office barely had enough time to generate the support
against the bill, and it was defeated last week by a margin
of only one vote. Twohy said, "We really had to hustle on
that one, as there was only a week between hearings.
Women
The first of the bills approved declared the "legislative
intent" that the Regents take immediate steps to increase
enrollment of women into UC's graduate schools so "the
percentage of women more nearly reflects the percentage
of women in California."
The lobby's letter of support reads, in part: "We think it a
remarkable waste of human skills and talent that women
have so long been discouraged from full participation in the
serious activity of society."
The committee also approved a bill to authórize the UC
Ftegents and the State College Trustees to establish-and

maintain child-care centers on UC and State college
campuses.
Children
Twohy wrote to the committee, "The lack of reasonably
inexpensive, properly supervised child-care centers forces
poor persons-in particular young mothers— to cancel their
dreams for a better education, and deprives the society of
the skills and talents they could develop at the University."
Student governments from the UC campuses originally
provided $12,000 for the lobby to begin operations. Twohy
estimates the student lobby will elose down on July 1 should
no more funding become available. A full-scale operation,
with student interns and a University-wide communications
system to reach the 100,000 UC students, is budgeted at over
$70,000 per year. The office presently does not even have a
secretary.
Twohy hopes funding will come from both student
government and private, sources. Keith Schiller, undergraduate student body. president, will introduce a
funding proposal for the lobby at next week's SLC meeting.
Interns
The Student lobby is also accepting applications for those
who wish to serve as student interns, without pay, over the
"We just don't have any money for
summer. Twohy said,
salaries, although if someone does have real financial need
and wants to do this, he should say so on the application."
Students should apply through the president's office,
Kerckhoff Hall 304.
Twohy said, "I think we're starting to show if students
decide to move this crazy system, it's possible to produce
the right results."

entries.title: Informal survey of BOC members shows Child Care cut likely
entries.author: Kenneth Kahn
entries.text:
Informal survey of
BOC members shows
Child Care cut likely
By Kenneth Kahn
Staff Writer
The Child Care Center will probably not be funded by ASUCLA
next year - seriously jeopardizing the center's existence -
an informal Daily Bruin suryey of Board of Control members shows.
ASUCLA provides about one-fifth of the center's $210,000 annuai
budget.
Of the ten member board, seven have indicated that they are
leaning toward voting for a proposal by BOC member Robert David
which would cut off ASUCLA monies for the controversial center.
If BOC votes to discontinues their portions of the center's funding,
Chancellor Young will probably withdraw about $27,000 of his funds
to Child Care. The program's supporters have argued that the center
cannot give decent care unless it receives full funding from all its
‹ current sources.
The Child Care Center presently receives matching contributions
of about $41,000 from BOC and the Registration Fee Committee's
budget, about $27,000 from the Chancellor, with State contributions
making up the remainder of the center's budget.
The center was given a temporary reprieve two weeks ago when
the Reg Fee committee voted to recommend continued funding for
the center, but with a 10 percent cut from the current $41,000
amount.
However, at least one Reg Fee member has indicated that their
committee may reconsider its decison should BOC not match Reg
Fee's tecommended allocation.
Two diametrically-opposed proposals on the Child Care Center
will come before BOC on Friday: the David proposal to cut ASUCLA
funds for the center, and one by Hal Thompson, administration
representative to BOC, which would make funding of the center a
standard item in the annual ASUCLA budget.
The David proposal seems to be the more significant because if it
passes and Child Care funding is cut, the Thompson proposal would
cease to be an issue.
Currently the center is funded by ASUCLA out of "Net Income,"
the same pool that funds the Students' Store Bonus program.
Board members opposing ASUCLA allocation for the center base
their reasoning on arguments:
-Spending over $40,000, which comes from a student population
of about 30,000, to benefit less than 100 students is an unfair üse of
student funds.
-The center itself is cost-efficient. The $2,500 the center spends
per child, per nine-month school year is just too much money per
child.
Most BOC members stressed that they are not against the Child
Care Center, but that ASUCLA should not be involved in funding of
the center.

entries.title: First Child Care Support Day
entries.text:
first Child Care Support Day
The first "Child Care Support Day at UCLA" is scheduled from
10 am-2 pm today in Schoenberg Quad. The organizers of the
event, the-Child Care Advocates, have invited the entire campus
community to bring children to participate.
Carrie Rothstein-Fisch, one of the coordinators of the rally, said
that there will be activities for both children and adults, including
"magicians, clowns, mimes, first aid, petitions,and buttons."
Allison Wilcox, the administrator of the Center, said there was
no indication of how many participants would show up, but added,
"Il the weather's good, we expect a pretty good turnout."
According to organizers of the rally, petitions will be circulated
among those in attendance in support of expanded, subsidized
quality day care, and the event will conclude with a presentation of
signed petitions to Chancellor Charles E. Young at his office. A
spokesman for the group said "we have over 1,000 petitions now,
and by the end of the day we may have up to 2,000."
Rothstein-Fisch said she hopes the rally today will call attention
to the Child Care Center's rather precarious existence. "The
operation of the Center," she said, "which takes children from the
ages of two months to four years, has proven that campus child
care can succeed.
"The Associated Students of UCLA maintain the Center for the
benefit of students, staff and faculty, but receive no University
funds for support. The Center is continually in financial crisis
resulting in an underpaid staff with a high turnover rate."
Rothstein-Fisch pointed out that, at UC Berkeley, five
University-operated child care centers are in operation serving
300 children "with one half of all funds coming from University
subsidy."

entries.title: Child Care Center named in legal suit
entries.author: Dave Peden
entries.text:
Child Care Center named in legal suit
By Dave Peden
DB Staff Writer
A civil class action suit accusing the ASUCLA Child Care Center
(CCC) of following an illegal fee schedule and illegally discriminating
against needy students was filed by two student families in Los Angeles
Superior Court Wednesday.
Named as defendants in the action were ASUCLA, ASUCLA Executive
Director Donald E. Findley and the Regents of the University of
California.
The suit, filed by Karen and Paul Thomas and Lulu and Erwin
Washington, charges that the Child Care Center maintained a fee

schedule contrary to a'schedule mandated by state law. It also charges
the Center's'quota-type admission policy (55 per cent student users, 30-
per cent staff and 15 per cent faculty) discriminates against low-income
students who could more than fill up the Center's 80 full-time child care
slots.
Pem
ing
The plaintiffs maintain that fees charged to them and other lowincome families were illegal under the state's fee schedule, and that
ASUCLA collection of fees charged under their own schedule is illegal.
There are about 25 families affected by the suit who are "either former,
present or potential welfare recipients" who, under state law, are
eligible for free child care at the ASUCLA Center. The suit charges

ASUCLA with deliberately refusing to switch to the sliding fee schedule,
thus penalizing the needy families.
ASUCLA maintains, in defense, that the use of the sliding fee schedule
was not made mandatory by the state until December of last year, and
that the State Department of Education had issued conflicting directives
which left the CCC here under the impression they were in fact in
compliance with state law.
Continuing problem
Allison Wilcox, administrator for the Center, said, "They (the State
Department of.Education) knew we were not using the sliding fee
schedule, and they didn't instruct us to go on it till December, last year."
The problem involving the Thomas family has been continuing for
some time, according to ASUCLA management. Their debts had
gradually grown to about $600, and they were expelled from the Center
because of repeated failures to repay the money..
The other 25 families in a similar position have since settled their bills,
Pindley said, and are welcome at the Center. "Of all the families the
Thomases are the only ones who haven't settled with us," he said.
ASUCLA maintains the Thomas family agreed to pay the costs at the
time they entered the Center regardless of the state regulations. Findley
termed the suit "nearly unintelligible," and added that it is apparently
nothing more than an'attempt to avoid payment of the bill.
"Unresponsiveness'
Richard A. Paez, plaintiff's counsel, disagreed, saying the suit is an
attempt to regain monies collected illegally by the Associated Students
from welfare-assisted families who have children in the CCC. Paez said
he has repeatedly communicated to ASUCLA the nature of the Thomas
complaint, and the Association's "unresponsiveness" led to the actual
filing.
(Continued on Page 18)

entries.title: For child care center: Full time funds discussed
entries.author: Eric Mandel and Patrick Healy
entries.text:
For child care center
Full time funds discussed
By Eric Mandel & Patrick Healy
DB Staff-Writers
Registration Fee Committee (Reg Fee) this week
recommended the Chancellor allocate no
registration fees for a full-time child care center
after January 1, 1976, when the part-time child care
center is scheduled to begin operation.
The recommendation was made during a special
three hour meeting Tuesday afternoon on the issue
of child care funding. The matter was so
controversial that it required Reg Fee's first roll
call vote of the year, 5-3-1, to pass the motion.
Usually it simply decides by consensus.
In its child care proposal, the Administration
allocated $62,972 until June 1976 in registration fees
as part. of a tripartite matching plan including
ASUCLA and other Chancellor's funds. Reg Fee
recommended $23,332 for the full-time center until
January 1, 1976, when the remainder will go to the
new part-time center. After the vote they discussed
attaching a note to the motion explaining that the
funding of the full-time center will be reconsidered
during the January 1 budget adjustments. The
decision on the note will be made during next
Wednesday's meeting.
Last year Reg Fee recommended $41,000 be
llonated for e nart-time center. The money has not

been spent and will almost certainly go toward
supporting the full-time center.
The committee objected to what they felt is a
large amount of money being spent on a small
number of children. The full-time center will accomodate between 68 and 70 children with the parttime center being planned for 74.
Some committee-members felt the higher costs
were necessary to ensure that the center provide
child development services in addition to child care.
Reg Fee administration representative Charles
McClure thought the recommendation for cutting
full-time funds was ill-considered. He said, "The
motion was completely nonsensical and
ridiculous."
Reg Fee Chairman Mark Waldman refused. to
vote except to make or break a tie. However, he
regreted calling for the vote at the time he did. He
said, "It was a mistake. I just wanted to get the
damn thing over with."
Another administration representative, Barbara
Wade, left the meeting just before the vote. At the
previous Reg Fee meeting, she had suggested the
committee pass the Administration's $62,972
proposal, saying child care has been."com mitted to
death."

entries.title: Child care suit: another side
entries.author: Paul Worthman and Stephan Brier
entries.text:
Child care suit: another side
By Paul Worthman and Stephan Brier
The Daily Bruin article of April 29 concerning the
legal suit filed against the ASUCLA Child Care
Center fails to present adequately the reasons for
the suit and the legal and political questions involved
The issues raised by the suit (some of which are
still very much alive, contrary to the assertions of
ASUCLA management) date back to the fall of 1973,
as the reporter for the Bruin is well aware.
Satisfactory reporting to the campus community
should hardly be based primarily on the opinions of
opinion
ASUCLA management in its unprincipled efforts to
discredit and ridicule the low-income, minority
people for whom the suit was filed.
The suit was filed because of the refusal of
ASUCLA's Executive Director and Board of Control
to face their moral and legal fesponsibilities to
Child Care Center families under the terms of the
State grant for the period before January 1, 1974.
The ASUCLA Child Care Center received a grant
from the California Department of Education of
approximately $57,000 in June, 1972, based upon the
fact that 60 per cent of the Center's 75 families were
certified past, present or potential welfare
recipients under the provisions of Title IVA of the
Social Security Act. The purpose of this money was
to make it possible for these families to obtain low
cost or free child care at the Center by subsidizing
their fees.
In December, 1972, the Director of the CCC,
received notification of a mandatory sliding fee
scale to go into effect on January 1, 1973. At its

January meeting the Center's Board of Governance
discussed the implications of the State grant. The
Parent-Chairperson of the Board reported that
priority in admission would nave to go to potentially-certified families and that the Center's fee
schedule would have to be revised by the adoption of
a sliding fee schedule.
Some parent Board members raised the question
of how, under the terms of the grant, child care on
campus could be made available to those student,
staff, and faculty families who need sueh care but
who would not be certifiable welfare families (this
is still one of the major issues regarding the expansion of child care facilities on campus).
In reply to a suggestion that the CCC might reject
the grant, the Executive Director of ASUCLA
responded by pointing out that he saw the grant as à
means to reducé the Center's then-$45,000 deficit. It
must be pointed out however, that if the grant were
used as legally intended - to subsidize the fees of
low-income families - it could not affect the
Center's income, unless the Center's fee schedule
were changed.
ASUCLA management in no way, nor at any
time, informed Center parents of the implications
of the State grant for parent fees and admission
priorities for certified families. ASUCLA continued
to take the grant without reducing fees for lowincome, certified families or changing its fee
schedule.
ASUCLA management reapplied for the grant for
the fiscal year beginning July 1, 1973, and although
actual receipt of funds was delayed, the Center
operated under the budgetary assumption that the
grant was fortheoming and they could continue to.
keep the fee schedule the, same.

entries.title: Education course to stress work in Child Care Center
entries.author: Steve Rubin
entries.text:
Education course to stress
work in Child Care Center
By Steve Rubin
DB Staff Reporter
Many students today are finding it hard to relate to
the theoretical problems involved in classroom
discussions, without being able to discover the
feeling of relevance acheived by repeated field work,
according to Aleta Letwin, former interim director
of the ASUCLA Child Care Center.
She said this problem is exemplified in the School
of Education where students are taught many
theories and problems in child development but often
are unable to come into direct contact with their •
main subject - the child.
However this quarter students enrolled in Judith
Ramirez's Early Childhood Education course
(Education 423-Section 2) will be able to 'come into
direct contact with children, through the facilities of
the Child Care Center, according to Barbara Spencer, administrative coordinator of the center.
Letwin said the program will be of intrinsic value
to students, in that it will enable their classroom
discussions tò be based on experience, and will help
• the center utilize the tremendous resource of student
workers who will come from the classroom ready to
test the relevancy of their classroom theories on
child development.
The center. through its wide range of volunteer

helpers and facilities, provides for the full range of
needs of children from two months to five years old,
Letwin said. These include social needs, intellectual'
curiosity, an emotionally stable environment, and
physical needs (children being able to flex their
muscles in a fascinating environment.)
Students enrolled in Education 423, section 2, will
be involved in the center's many activities which
could be anything from telling a story to changing a
diaper. Students will also take trips with the
children. These are explorations, according to
Letwin, designed to utilize the many resources of the
campus community. Last quarter children saw a
special showing of Midsummers Night Dream,
watched glass blowers in action and fed the fish in
the botanical gardens.
Letwin said the new resevoir of talent from the
School of Education will help the child care center in
three ways: 1) it will provide more consistent hourly
participation to furnish the children with greater
care; 2) it will give the staff a more professional
outlook, there being more volunteers with a child
development background, rather than just unskilled
helpers; and 3) it will enable the child care center.to..
expand its program, enabling it to provide many
• more activities for the children.
Students interested in enrolling in the education
course should contact Ramirez in Moore Hall 302.

entries.title: Budget for child care Center passed by Board of Control
entries.author: Dave Peden
entries.text:
Budget for child care center
passed by Board of Control
By Dave Peden
DB Staff Writer
The ASUCLA Board of Control voted unanimously last night to -approve an ASUCLA Child Care Center (CCC) calling for expansion of the
Center here. The decision was made in a meeting which left somé child
care supporters worried, administration répresentatives puzzled about
"paranoia" among those supporters and the ultimate fate of the CCC up
in the air because of funding uncertainties.
The budget, generated by an ad hoc committee, proposed that the CCC
be expanded to serve 297 children in 169 full-time care slots, as opposed
to its present capacity of about 80 children in 69 slots: The 100 additional
slots are to be gained by development of two drop-in, part-time day care
centers which will operate in addition to the present full-time center.
Specifically, the Board recommended in the budget that funding for
the semtery mmeney fro m bot, Ahe Clesistral in iversty Comam, te oding
University Policies Commission and the Chancellor's office. That
recommendation follows the lead of UPC, which recommended such a
financial arrangement after lengthy study of the issue. BOC funding of
next year's Center is listed at $50,000 of its proposed operating loss of
-$150,049. The $50,000 is contingent upon additional funding from other
and ASUCLA
budget sources, their acceptance of the budget,
representation in the Center's realignment under the new funding
system.
There was some question over thé increased costs projected in the
büdget for next year, since this year's Center is budgeted to operate at
$25,000 loss and next year's Center will lose over five times that amount.
The major cost difference is an increase of about $75,000 in staff salaries,
said Maria Ramos, BOC undergraduate member and a long-time
supporter of on-campus day care here
Ramos said next year's salaries, after they are increased, will still be
too low. "'I went through the job ranges in the University and compared
them to what we've proposed," Ramos said. "Our master teacher will
make about as much asa senior computer operator, our associate
teacher as much as a principle baker or cook and our teacher $14 less per
month than an outside window washer." Ramos noted.
There was a great deal of concern expressed, both among Board
members and those in the large audience, that the budget will not be
approved in principle by the University or other funding source in time
for an application for state funds to be submitted
The formal deadline for State money was May 1, over two weeks ago,
but "we have obtained an oral extension until early next week,'
cording to Donald Findley, ASUCLA executive director. The state is
expected to contribute $53,867 to the Center next year, but if the Center's
request is deemed too late to be considered, or if the request is denied,
the proposed Center deficit will be over $200,000, and would result in the
total burden being shared only on campus by the Associated Students
and the University.
Since the State has requested a budget by next week, the University
and ASUCLA must agree on the final funding of the CCC before that
time.
Ramos said, "I'd like to send up this budget but I'd like to sit down with
the University and work out the details. I feel a slight tendency to avoid
the issue and postpone it," Ramos continued. "ASUCLA must make a
decision soon, if not, we're going to get stuck. It's time to sit down and
work it out very quickly," she added.
Another major concern with the funding situation, not as acute but
apparently just as important, is the possibility that the University will in
fact not come up with the necessary funds.
(Continued on Page 22)

entries.title: Young supported on child care stand
entries.author: Nyle Kardatzke
entries.text:
Young supported on child care stand

Editor:
Chancellor Young should not try
to be subtle with the Child Care
Center Committee. He should tell
them directly that it is
preposterous and unfair for them
to expect other students to assume
responsibility for their children.
The same illogic could lead me to
demand that "the University"
(meaning all the students) open a
Car Care Center for the maintenance of old cars like my own.
Aside from the illogic of shifting
responsibility for children to
people other than the parents,
consider one of the budgets the
Committee itself has mentioned
(DB, Nov. 11): $275,000 • for 122
children. That's $2,254 per child.
If all 2800 kids mentioned by the
Committee are cared for at that
cost, the bill would amount to
$6,311,200. This comes to about $210
per UCLA student if the money
were from University funds.
If each child is attached to one
student- parent, every such parent
would be receiving a gift of $2,044
from the childless students. What
principle of equity could justify
such a scheme?
Suppose some rationalization
can be conceived for parents not

raising their own children. And
suppose it is acknowledged that
much of the $275,000 (or $6,311,200)
may be for long-lasting physical
facilities, not just operating costs.
And suppose the cost per child falls
as more are added so that
$6,311,200 is an exaggeration.
Granting all these points, it is still
not clear why current childless
students owe a "debt" not only to
present student-parents but also to
those who would use the facility in
the future.
Maybe the Committee should
plan a bond issue to finance the
physical facilities of the Child Care
Emporium they clamor for. Then
they could still lobby for diversion
of University funds
from
educational to babysitting purposes. And, hopefully, Chancellor
Young would continue to thwart
them.
Nyle Kardatzke
Grad, Economics

entries.title: Child care
entries.author: Don Norman
entries.text:
Child care
Editor:
Judy Kunofsky evidently does
not realize it, but she has spoken
out in favor of overpopulation. As

president of the Zero Population
Growth movement, Miss Kunofsky
should oppose, not favor, a UCLA
free child care center.
Most families find children quite
adorable, and if the cost of having
them is lowered, not only in terms
of food and clothing expenditures,
but also in taking care of them,
why not have more? The free child
care center gives such an incentive.
Judy may be able to persuade
her friends in ZPG not to have
more children, but I suspect most
people aren't in fear over, imminent overpopulation.
Besides, history is replete with
examples where price incentives to
do something completely swamp
the counter effects of moral
suasion to do otherwise.
Don Norman
Grad, English

By Dave Peden

A bill which would allocate $3 million in state funds to support oncampus child care programs was introduced into the State Assembly
Tuesday by its co-sponsors, John Vasconcellos (D-Santa Clara) and
Frank/Lanterman (R- Los Angeles).
The bill AB 4190, would fund child care centers at public institutions of
higher learning throughout the state, and would almost triple the
number of campus child care programs receiving state funding in
California. Presently only 19 campus child care centers are aided with
state monies, while over 50 centers applied for such aid.
AB 4190 would, if passed, significantly improve the financial status of

Presently, not only are child care centers prohibited from using parent

reverse the ruling.

entries.title: Once doomed child-care center appears to be making comeback
entries.text:

appears to be making comeback
By Joanne Eglash
Editor-in-chief
The see-saw that the controversial UCLA Child
Care Services has. been riding for the last few
years seems to have tilted recently in their favor.
In a move that one child-care proponent
termed "a significant change in the administration's feelings." Chancellor Young has
committed himself to covering any deficit in the
UCLA Development Center's goal of raising
$20,000 in private contributions this year for
child-care services.
And the Registration Fee Committee, whose
members last year voted to cut its share of
funding for the center by 50 percent, has
expressed its concern about the facilities.
Young had previously ordered the center
closed as of last Sept. I. After intervention from
Undergraduate President Dean Morehous and
Graduate President Dahlstedt, however, he gave
the child-care center until Nov. 17 to develop an

alternative plan for child care consistent with a
series of modifications including a reduction
of costs through lower salaries and volunteers,
operation by an agency other than the campus
administration and increased income - set forth
in a letter of understanding.
The Aug. 30 letter of understanding also called
for creation of the Child Care Study Group,
consisting of representatives from the administration, faculty, staff, staff union, parents and
students. The group is required to make written
progress reports. on the status of the planning
effort.
Much of the group's efforts must concentrate
on funding, in accordance with the chancellor's
request for an essentially self-supporting plan. In
their first two progress reports, the study group
announced a revised fee schedule, greater
parental involvement, a nearly tripled use of
volunteers, and a variety of fund-raising efforts.
